speechtext:

subtopic: WAR DISABILITY PENSIONS TO IMPERIAL VETERANS
WAR DISABILITY PENSIONS TO IMPERIAL VETERANS
speechtext:
1.	What representations, if any, have been made by this government to the British govern-
[Mr_ E. Lapointe.]
ment with respect to an increase of war disability pensions payable to imperial veterans of the great war now residing in Canada?
2.	If any such representations have been so made, what were the nature and character of same ?
3.	What has been the attitude of the British government with respect to such representations?
4.	Will this government consider the arrangement of a conference with the British government for the purpose of further discussing the above matter?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: WAR DISABILITY PENSIONS TO IMPERIAL VETERANS
speechtext:
During the session of 1936 there was set up a committee on pensions and returned soldier problems. During the course of the hearing before the committee strong representations were made by exsoldiers who had served in the imperial forces, at present residing in Canada, to the effect that representations should be made on their behalf to the British government. During that summer, while on the trip to Vimy, I had occasion to discuss with officers of the British Ministry of Pensions the situation with respect to these ex-imembers of the imperial forces. I made certain informal representations. As a result of these representations I came to the conclusion that no particular encouragement would 'be given to the idea that there should be special recognition for ex-imperial soldiers now residing in Canada. The British government, or representatives of the British government with whom I discussed the matter, felt at that time that it would not be fair to ex-service men residing in other dominions that special favours or special privileges should be accorded to ex-mem'bers of the forces in Canada.
As to the fourth question, this is a matter of government policy, and I do not think it has a place on the order paper.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS

speechtext:
The house resumed from Friday, April 29, consideration in committee of Bill No. 105, to assist in the alleviation of unemployment and agricultural distress-Mr. Rogers-Mr. Sanderson in the chair.
On section 1-Short title.
Mr. WrOODSWORTH: Mr. Chairman, this bill is along the lines of the legislation of previous years. I should like to get the minister if possible to state whether the administration is to be along the line of previous years. Since the discussion on Friday the report of the dominion commissioner of unemployment relief has been distributed. Surely it is not too much to ask the minister whether he proposes to proceed along similar lines next year. When legislation of this kind was first introduced it was confessedly emergency legislation; it included drought relief and unemployment relief. ' Drought is due to natural causes-according to the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett), due to an act of God. Unemployment, on the other hand, is undoubtedly due to the blundering of man. I do not know why the two should again be put together this year.

Since unemployment can no longer be regarded as an emergency, it should not be dealt with by an emergency measure. Let us take the figures-and I am speaking now of relief apart from drought. I notice that in March, 1934, the numbers assisted, as reported by the provinces and the federal departments, excluding the drought areas, totalled 1,205,863; in March 1935, the number was 1,172,246; in March 1936, 1,240,074; and in March 1937. 1,045,766. Then unemployment dropped until in September of that year the number assisted was 543,336; but since that time the numbers on relief have been steadily increasing until we are back again in March to 848,497. So that the problem, far from having been solved, seems to be again on the increase.
I submit that this type of relief is haphazard. It bears every mark of an improvised scheme and is wholly inadequate; there are many gaps and many people are suffering. Take transients. The development of this country called for a large number of unskilled or semi-skilled workmen, a huge mobile army that could be readily transported from one province to another. This army still exists, but its members cannot establish residence in any one province. That is the difficulty. There are some 4,000 of them now roaming the streets of Vancouver; many of them belong no more to Vancouver than to Ontario or Saskatchewan or Alberta. They are part of that great army. Vancouver city ought not to be called upon to take care of them, nor should the province of British Columbia, and jret this government looks to the province to do this sort of thing. It will be said, of course, that the difficulty is inherent in our constitution, but it seems to me that we must find some way to get around it.
Since the discussion on Friday two memoranda have been sent to me from my own city of Winnipeg, one pleading for highway construction, and the other for help in the repairing and erection of school buildings. It may be said that under the British North America Act school buildings are obviously a school responsibility; but the province is almost bankrupt; and after all, why should we have expenditures on unneeded barracks, and not have expenditures on needed homes? WThy should we have ornate public buildings in one part of the country, while in another part of the country we are not able to provide even for schools and hospitals?
The hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) in the discussion the other day spoke in favour of projects for youth training. I quite agree with him, but I would point out that the training of youth is worth very

Relief and Agricultural Distress
little unless it is supplemented by work for the young people so trained. Are we going to have to wait and wait until possibly a war breaks out or some other catastrophe of that kind overtakes us before granting to our youth what seems to me to be their inherent right, an opportunity to work?
There is another matter I wish to mention in this connection and that is unemployment insurance. It ought to be an integral part of any scheme of this kind. The government promised that measure very definitely at the last election. They are pledged to unemployment insurance. I do not think they can very well escape responsibility by saying that one or two provinces object to the scheme. The problem is still there. Ways and means were found, in regard to old age pensions, whereby the measure was actually put into operation even though a number of the provinces were opposed: and now even the provinces that were opposed at that time have fallen into line. We have a right to ask the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) or the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) who is now in his seat, to tell us whether the government proposes at this session to bring down unemployment insurance.
We hear a great deal from members of this house about the pioneering spirit. We are told that a great many of the unemployed ought to get out and work as the pioneers did. But surely anyone who makes this statement must realize that conditions are very different now from the conditions under which our pioneering forefathers came to this country and established homes for themselves. They were able to push into the wilderness, to conquer new territory, to discover new resources and to invent new methods. Why should not. we in this house exhibit the pioneer spirit? It seems to me that it is our duty in these days to do pioneering in our modern industrial, commercial and social environment. What is the use of following along day after day, week after week, year after year, the old principle of giving doles to beggars? If we had one-tenth of the spirit of the pioneers we in this house would invent some new way of dealing with unemployment.
As I said on Friday, I hesitate to criticize the Minister of Labour in this fashion, because there is no member of the cabinet for whom I have a higher regard; but I must insist that the government must be held responsible for this situation. The hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Bradette) I believe it was, pleaded for cooperation. We are very willing to cooperate, but every member of the house knows that members in opposition-for that matter any private member

cannot bring in a money
bill. We know that according to the composition of the house the government has an enormous majority, and the government in taking office takes the responsibility of dealing with this situation. I do not think the minister is justified in simply bringing in an enabling bill without giving us a very much fuller explanation than he has hitherto done of what the department and the government propose to do with this question, which he himself admits is one of the most important questions before the Canadian people to-day.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
Before the clause carries I hoped that the minister might have given an answer to my hon. friend's question. The other evening I discussed the question of relief allowances, and the minister informed me at that time that the government have very little control over the amount of relief that is granted. I do not know exactly what methods are adopted by the department to control the amount of relief granted in the various municipalities. But in introducing this measure a few weeks ago the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) referred to the fact that there are certain districts in Canada where it was claimed that the relief scales were too high, or were competing in recent years with the labour market. When I raised this question the other night I had in mind the fact that in the Winnipeg district those in charge of the granting of relief were laying down certain scales of expenditures to apply to persons who, previously in receipt of relief, were working either on public projects or in private undertakings. I gave figures showing how much the recipients of relief were receiving. Now I am going to give the amount that a person working is allowed to spend. I want the committee to understand the importance of the implications of an organization laying down limits to the amount which persons who happen to have been in receipt of public relief may spend.
In Winnipeg the amount allowed to a husband and wife on relief was S12.76 for rood and S14.17 for rent, light, etc., making a total of $26.93 per month. Of course this does not include a great many things which are necessary to existence, such as clothing. According to the rules being laid down for the Winnipeg district it appears that if the husband is working the <;ouple will not be allowed to spend more than $50 per month. If they do, and if they go on relief again, they will find themselves penalized. For a household of five persons the maximum expenditure allowed is $80 per month. If they spend more and subsequently have to go on relief-and such greater expenditures may be unavoidable by reason of sickness for example

Relief and Agricultural Distress
-they will not be given public relief unless they can show to the relief commission exactly how that money has been spent. Now in this a vital principle is involved, and the government cannot absolve itself of responsibility. The minister claims that in some districts the scale of relief is too high, so he must have had something in mind. And when relief bodies lay down regulations as to how much a month a person who has received relief may spend, they are interfering with the standard of living in a way in which I think it ought not to be done by any public body. I should like to know whether the government are in any way responsible for these regulations. If they are not directly responsible I would ask the minister whether the government have approved of any of these regulations by control over the amount of money that is spent in any municipality.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Taking up first the question raised by the hon. member who has just spoken, the determination of relief allowances has always remained with the municipalities, subject to provincial regulations. In the agreements between the dominion and the provinces covering the grants in aid, as I indicated last week, provision was made during the last quarter of the past year that the relief scales should not exceed the normal earnings of the individual or family. The intention of that was to prevent relief scales competing with the labour market. Apart from that we have not exercised any control whatsoever over the relief allowances in the various provinces and the municipalities within the provinces, nor do we approve the specific regulations made in the municipalities. My hon. friend will understand that those who are closest to the situation are in a far better position to do that than any officials of the dominion Department of Labour would be. There is a great diversity of relief allowances across this country from Prince Edward Island to Vancouver, and. as I pointed out before, even within the provinces there is great diversity. I know of no way in which you can deal with that satisfactorily under existing conditions except to leave it with the municipalities who are primarily concerned.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Does the minister approve of these municipal or other bodies associated with the granting of relief laying down rules as to the amount a family may spend during the time they are off relief?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
There is also a provision in the recent agreements with the provinces whereby there may be assistance through budgeting during the time they are off relief, in order that those who had been on relief

may be helped to spend their earnings in the most provident way. The whole intention is rather to give assistance to those who have been on relief, not to embarrass or handicap them in their reestablishment.
May I return to the series of questions raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth). I have no doubt they will be raised again in another form after we get beyond the title clause of the bill.
The first point he raised was with regard to the wisdom of separating agricultural relief from unemployment relief. In that connection he referred particularly to relief in the drought areas. He may not have been in the house the other day when I pointed out that when we were obliged to meet a recurrence of the drought situation in the autumn of last year it was decided that it would be preferable that the administration of direct relief in the drought areas should be placed where the administration of other forms of relief in the drought areas had already been placed, namely with the Department of Agriculture. That has been done, and will be continued.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
I understood that,
but why bring in an omnibus bill which includes these very diverse types of relief in one measure ?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
The reason lies in the
fact that we proceed under the broad provisions of this bill to enter into agreements with the various provinces concerning the administration of particular forms of relief. For instance during the past year we would normally have had as many as five agreements with the western provinces covering direct relief, youth training, joint works projects, and the various forms of drought relief. Under the broad provisions of this bill we enter into agreements with the provinces covering the various measures of relief.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: What about transients?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
We have dealt with the
provinces. We have recognized that transients ought not to be a direct burden upon the municipalities. At the same time there has been during the past teii years a constant movement of transients back and forth across the country.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
For the past
twenty-five years or more.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
I am willing -to
agree that it has gone on much beyond ten years. It has been a feature of the growth of this country, as my hon. friend has said.

Relief and Agricultural Distress
But in other years these transients might have been regarded as seasonal workers. They were usually able, at least they were willing, to find seasonal work which would carry them through the year without having to depend in any way upon state assistance. During the very severe years of the recent depression provision was made for these single unemployed transients by me'ans of the relief camps established under the Department of National Defence. As many as 25,000 of these single unemployed were sheltered in these camps during the winter months. As my hon. friend is aware, that number was reduced very much during the summer months, in fact many of the camps were closed during that period. We prepared for that situation in a way which is fully understood by hon. members of the committee and I shall not go into it in great detail at this time.
We provided that the dominion and the provinces would assume responsibility for caring for these single homeless men during the winter months. This has been done by means of the farm employment plan in the prairie provinces and the forestiy conservation camps in British Columbia. In all cases these plans have operated within restricted seasons of the year, normally from mid-October until April or May. When the severe winter season had passed many of those who had found temporary shelter or employment under these plans for transients went to various occupations of a seasonal nature. By means of these plans we have stabilized the problem, at least during the winter months, at which time it used to be very severe.
I am sure the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre will agree that the provisions made during the last two or three years for the single unemployed under the farm employment plan have certainly reduced the number who would have been receiving meals at the centres where meals were given out in Winnipeg. I have seen the figures and I am sure he is fully aware of that fact, regardless of what opinion he may have of the plan. We have undertaken that burden in conjunction with the provinces and naturally we have followed the advice of the provincial authorities as to what plans were best suited to their needs.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: With regard to the situation in British Columbia, I do not think it was adequately dealt with by the minister's statement. Why should the province in which a man happens to find himself when up against it have to be burdened with his care when he is not able to establish residence? The various offices having to do with social work generally insist that a man must establish residence before he comes under a certain scheme, but I do not think these men are any more a responsibility of a particular province than they are of any other province in which they may have happened to be for the last two or three years.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
That principle has never applied to any of the projects intended to care for the single homeless unemployed men. We have never applied a strict residence qualification. In British Columbia there has been a restriction as to the date beyond which a transient entering the province would not be employed on a particular project. That restriction was applied with the full approval of the provincial authorities. We have applied the most liberal residence provisions in connection with the employment of transients, either on the special projects or under the farm employment plan. As a matter of fact it is very difficult to determine the domicile of many of these transients in British Columbia. According to the latest report I have seen, of a total number of, say, 4,000 previously employed in the forestry conservation camps in British Columbia, possibly 1,800 came from outside the province. The presumption is that the remainder could establish domicile in British Columbia. However, there are two forms of transiency, transiency within the province and that which might be termed interprovincial transiency. There is a movement from city to city within a province and a movement from one province to another. That is why in dealing with that special aspect of the general problem we have tried to meet the provinces upon the basis of our accepting with them the responsibility for the care of these transients through the severe winter months. Our past experience has shown that during the summer months, when seasonal employment is available, it is not necessary to .provide this type of employment.
There is another thing which has been made perfectly clear from our experience and to which I am sure my hon. friend will agree. If you establish more favourable conditions for employment for a certain type of transient in one province than for another, you at once aggravate the problem in that province. You cannot give preferential treatment to a particular group of unemployed. In other words, you could not readily defend the establishment of works projects which would be confined exclusively to a particular group. That is why in suggesting works projects in other yehrs we have made them as readily available to married heads of families on relief as to the single unemployed.

Relief and Agricultural Distress

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Is there any reason why the city of Vancouver should be forced to care for these single unemployed transients who are not from Vancouver? As the minister has just said, a large proportion of them are not even from British Columbia. Is there any reason why the citizens of Vancouver should have to pay for these men during the few weeks in the spring after the camps close and in the fall before the forestry camps are open?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: My impression is that the municipalities generally have not been held responsible for the care of these men apart from special projects. Assistance is given by the dominion to the provinces through grants in aid which are supposed to cover relief generally within the province, in no way excluding what may be done for these single unemployed men.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: These men cannot be allowed to starve. They go out with tin cans to collect money and many of them have been put in gaol. They have developed quite a technique in collecting money in the city. The result is that the citizens have to pay. Surely the dominion government should be able to make some provision to prevent the placing of this burden upon the citizens of the city. This condition is worse in Vancouver than in any other part of Canada. I believe we have more transients who drift into the city. I urge the minister to endeavour to find a solution for this problem, which arises every year.	-

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
When I spoke during the debate on the second reading of this bill on Friday last I drew to the attention of the house the situation existing in Vancouver. I pointed out that at the end of March this year there were approximately 6,900 persons on relief, that is, heads of families and single unemployed transients, but not including dependents of heads of families. I pointed out also that that was about one thousand less than at the same time last year. To take effect either on March 15 or April 1 the provincial government is compelling the cities and municipalities of British Columbia to take over the burden of the relief of a considerable number who heretofore have been cared for by the province. I received yesterday from Vancouver a statement of the number of cases and the monthly expenditures in connection with their keep. While at the end of March of this year the number of cases was one thousand less than last year, beginning with the first, of April 3,445 new cases have been placed on the relief list in the city of Vancouver. I presume that other cities and

municipalities had additions to their lists as well, but I am not conversant with that.
It is quite impossible for the city of Vancouver with falling revenues to take care of the increasing numbers of relief cases. The monthly cost for these 3,445 persons is computed at $34,072; that is for food, clothing and shelter, and does not take into account medical attention and other incidentals. The method that is now being followed in my opinion will never deal with the unemployment situation definitely or satisfactorily. We have to realize that the people can get their sustenance only from the industries of the country. It does not matter how it comes to them; it comes from industry in the last analysis, and this government will have to tell the owners of . industry that either they must so operate their industries that they will support the people of this country, or the government will organize industry for that purpose.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: How can they do it?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: How otherwise are you going to end unemployment?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: How are you going to operate industry if you have not any business?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: If it is not the business of industry to operate their industries to support the people of this country, what is it?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: To make money.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: I am glad to get that answer. I have been telling this house for the last eight years that under the capitalist system the function of industry is to make profits for the owners of industry. But to-day industry cannot make profits for its owners and at the same time supply the people with the goods they need. That is the very thing that the government of this country and of every capitalist country has to face. I do not say that it is an easy problem to solve, that it can be taken care of offhand by just making a statement in this house or anywhere else; I am satisfied that it cannot be taken care of until we reorganize industry to perform the functions that industry was intended to perform. In the solution of that problem I am prepared to assist either by saying nothing or by helping in any other way that I can.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: May I suggest to the hon. gentleman that the best way to do that sort of thing is to put a little money into industry and hire some people, and try it out.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
This is not the time to go into that point. It does not make any difference how much money you put into

Relief and Agricultural Distress
industry unless industry distributes the means of purchasing the goods produced. The difficulty we are met with to-day is that too much of the fruits of industry or of the income created by industry go to people who do not need it and cannot use it, and they cannot put it into new industry. There is any amount of money available in the Dominion of Canada and any amount of money available in the United States to double our industries, but we cannot dispose of the products because the people have not the means to buy them.
The Minister of Labour said a few moments ago that in dealing with the unemployment situation the government had to be careful that they did not give a scale of relief higher than the wages paid in industry, because otherwise there would be a tendency for people to go on relief and keep away from work. These things have been said before. Before rising to speak I said to one of my colleagues that all this discussion seems so futile. I feel the futility of it all, because until we are prepared really to examine the fundamental basis of our economic and social structure and grapple with the problems which have arisen in that social and economic structure, we are not going to find the solution to the problem.
Two or three years ago I read the report of the Hoover committee in the United States, a very conservative committee set up by President Hoover in 1932, and reporting in 1934. While I speak entirely from memory I recall that that very conservative committee reported that if the industrial equipment of the United States, the labour then available, and the natural resources, were properly organized and utilized for the good of the American people, they could provide goods and services which would give to every family of five persons an average standard of living such as was then enjoyed by those who received incomes of over $4,000 per year.
That was a startling statement. We too have the resources; we have the equipment; we have the labour. Yet, under our present economic structure, leaving it to competitive industry-which, as the Minister of Agriculture showed, does not exist any more because another factor has entered into the economic structure which has set aside the old law of supply and demand-there is no cure. Perhaps if we could go back to that old law we might get a new start; but we cannot go back Society never does.
My purpose in rising is to emphasize the fact that fundamental changes must come, a fact with which I believe the minister must be familiar. I urge upon the minister and government to consider these matters in the light of new conditions which have arisen in the last twenty-five years, and to bring before us proposals not for the continuance of relief but for the elimination of unemployment and of the necessity of continuing to provide relief for persons who are able-bodied and ready and willing to work on the land, in the forests, in the mines, or in industry and elsewhere.

The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) is an exceedingly able speaker. The house listens to him with rapt attention and then-I believe I am safe in following him and saying what he said-it agrees to do precisely nothing.

For a moment or two I should like to go back to 1930, and attempt to analyse the differences existing between 1930 and 1937. These, in my view, are the main causes of the unemployment we have to-day. In 1930 we had a one per cent sales tax, while in 1937 we had an eight per cent sales tax. In 1930 we had no excise tax, now we have a three per cent excise tax, in reality a tariff of that amount, upon all goods coming from foreign countries. In addition to that we have a tariff which has reached heights never before approached in Canadian history. It is so high that I feel quite certain neither the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) nor the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) could by any possibility look over the top of it.
We now have a tariff framed upon a new basis. Our customs tariff, which records the rates for the Dominion of Canada, is now distributed with blank pages interspersed here and there throughout the book. The object of the blank pages is to provide a place on which one may write the real tariff, because the tariff schedule as it stands does not reveal the true situation. One must get the true rate from the customs branch by a special statement. Even then I venture to assert that if to-day I were to ask the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Ilsley) the tariff on certain items of cotton goods from the United States he would have to tell me, "Well, it is recorded in the book." But one must then add three per cent to the tariff, and a further eight per cent sales tax, and then if one wishes to follow it through to the last he would be told that in addition section 36 of the Customs Act has to be considered, through which special values are imposed upon products coming from the United States. To a certain extent that value depends upon the humour of the man who makes the valuation or, to go back to an old phrase, the rate of customs duty depends upon the length of the chancellor's boot.
I venture to suggest to the Minister of Labour, the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister that if we were to return to the tariff and taxation levels of 1930 our unemployment problem would be solved. We are diverting a large amount of the earnings of our people from the purchase of consumers' goods to expenditures upon relief, railways and other things, and there is not left a sufficient sum to provide a normal purchasing power for the people of Canada.
When we consider these problems what do we do? The suggestions are many and varied. One man says we ought to provide unemployment insurance. Not long ago in the house I explained that after careful calculation I

Relief and Agricultural Distress
had found the earnings of the farmer amounted to S362 per year while the earnings of the labourer in industry amount to well over $900 per year. And so if we provided unemployment insurance we would be setting up further taxation upon people receiving less than $400 in order to provide insurance for those receiving more than $900. You are proposing to expend money upon public works, but I ask, when you have expended money upon public works, unless they render a direct serviceable value, unless they have an exchange value to the community, unless they assist in the movement of commodities or in some way in improving the efficiency of our services in the Dominion of Canada, what have you? You have men temporarily employed in a particular business and as soon as that is over they have no employment. But if on the other hand we made some effort to reduce taxation so that we could free some of this money which is now spent upon taxation, I venture to assert that your unemployment would dissolve like the early cloud in the morning dew.
But, as the previous speaker has said, we hear all these things but parliament never comes to grips with them. No one will answer the statement that I have made now. No one will meet me and try to disperse-if I may use that term-or deny or meet the arguments that I have made. I do not agree with my hon. friend the previous speaker; I do not accept his conception that we can abolish unemployment by nationalizing industry or anything of that kind; but I should like to see his arguments met and I should like to see parliament actually consider this problem instead of going on as we are doing day after day-discussing, listening, many of us, perhaps all of us, in earnest, but very few, I am sorry to say, perhaps none of us knowing where to go.
I turned over to-day by chance the last page of The Count of Monte Cristo. It is, I think, the strongest closing of any novel I have ever read: The Count sends his message and he says, "The greatest of all human wisdom is to wait and hope." Well, it may be something by way of a philosophy to go through life with charming ease and patience and say, "We shall wait and hope. We shall not do anything to solve the problems. We shall simply wait and hope." But I want something just a little different. I want something done to-day. I want some consideration of these problems in order that something may be accomplished in our own time. This is what I ask the house. This is what I know the country asks of us.

Yesterday was May 1, and upon that occasion throughout the world many workers united in order to discuss their various problems. But what appeared to me most striking was the news which came from Germany of a speech made by Hitler on the occasion of his addressing hundreds of thousands of persons. This is what he said, in effect. "The so-called democracies of the world have been laughing at fascism for the past five years. They have thought that what we were trying to do was a ridiculous thing. Well, I say to them that there are no idle hands in Germany; there are not sufficient hands to do the work, that we wish to have done. Meanwhile, although the so-called democracies have yet to-solve their problem of unemployment, they presume to laugh at us." I say, because I believe it is a timely matter to mention, that in various parts of Canada we are seeing the rise of fascism. Why? Simply because of inaction. It is because these democratic institutions that we should like to preserve are represented by people who are either unable or unwilling to grapple with the problems we have to face. It is unquestionably true that in the so-called democracies of the world* -and I speak particularly of Canada, the country I know best-the problem of unemployment has not been solved, nor has any attempt yet been made at a solution. As the-hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar has stated, the preamble to this bill is ample evidence that the present situation will be permitted to continue.

If the profits came from anywhere, they came from the prices obtained for the products produced. However, the government has a remedy against that condition by way of taxation. In that way this wealth is being redistributed to some extent.
One of these companies is spending millions of dollars in northern Canada, much of it in Saskatchewan, in developing new mining prospects and setting up mining plants. I do not know where the company could have got the money to do this work except out of the profits that had been accumulated at other times. not like questions to be asked of them. They want to spend their time reading quotations from books they do not understand or have not thought their way through. They have not yet come to the conclusion which is held by reasonable and intelligent people that two and two always make four. They have always some magic formula to make two and two eight, or sometimes three. If they would devote a little more time to thinking and a little less to reading quotations they would get along better.
It is not within the responsibility of the Minister of Labour to make easier for us at the moment the means of exchange of wealth or the bringing into this country of goods to pay for goods that go out, and so on this bill I am not going to advise the minister as to that. I do not think it would be in order in any event. I should like to back up the plea of the hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deachman) that as quickly as possible reductions should be made in taxation for the purpose of leaving that wealth with people who can make better use of it than any government can do. Let it stay in the hands of private individuals who will use it for productive purposes, rather than have it collected and spent by the government.
I should like to say to the minister, and I am sure he will agree with me, that in the disbursement of money in accordance with the terms of this measure every effort should be made to see that the money is spent for the most useful public works-works that will be of value and available for the enjoyment and profit and pleasure of all people. I do not think that buildings in large cities fall within that category. I do not think housing schemes carried out by the government fall within that category. The government cannot build houses for all the people; they must select the recipients of the houses they build. It is all right for the government to help housing schemes under strict regulations so that anyone who comes within the regulations and meets with the requirements can get the benefits of the scheme, but to say that the government should step in and provide houses for all the people of Canada, well, that is not the spirit that built up Canada or will continue to build it up from now on.
There are works that can be done to advantage at the present time. Labour is plentiful, and there is no great demand for excessive wages for the necessary labour to take care of these improvements that would benefit all the people. Equipment is reasonably plentiful. It has not been in use for a long time, and not much equipment would be needed. The original Hudson Bay railway was largely built by men with wheelbarrows and shovels.

That was all the equipment they needed. Furthermore, I believe it was built at about as low a cost as it could be done to-day with much more modern machinery. The difference in cost between doing work by that method, which looks antiquated, and by the most modern machinery, is not so great as might appear on the surface. In any case the money spent in that way went directly into the pockets of labour, which was better than having the work done by machinery and using machinery supplies, the benefit of which would go elsewhere. I am not one of those who believe that machinery does away with the opportunities for labour, but it does dislocate the demand for labour and causes additional work to be provided in some other part of the country rather than in the part where the machine is actually working.
So Mr. Chairman, I believe that on highway construction and road construction through new territory, in our mining country, and in the building of parks around our cities and towns, and in other works of the kind, much help may be given. Those not on relief should not be prevented from getting work of this kind. Many who are not on relief have kept off the relief lists simply by their own efforts and determination, and encouragement should be given to them to stay off by providing them with some of this work at wages comparable to those paid in similar industries in the district in which the work is being done. That wage policy would also help to ensure that those who have jobs shall not quit them to get government work.
It might possibly help the minister if I gave him more advice, but I am reminded of the wise man who prayed something like this: Oh Lord, save me from my friends; I can look after my enemies myself.

This section deals with the power to appropriate moneys for the purposes of the act. There is one subject I should like to bring to the attention of the Minister of Labour, and it is this: When a similar measure was up for discussion last year, I remember speaking to the minister with respect to the Monkman pass project, a project which concerns approximately 70,000 people located in the Peace River country. As we find out we can get no assistance from any government whatsoever, I should like to tell the minister what has been done in that particular instance. I should like, too, to answer the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. McLean) who maintains that if people want to go out and work, they can easily find it. May I point out that this is one occasion where people have already tried to help themselves.
It is a known fact that there is no outlet to the Pacific coast from the Peace River district. For many years we have sought an outlet by railway. We have come to realize slowly, but nevertheless reluctantly, that at the present time such an outlet is not to be expected. The people of that country realize that if they cannot get a rail outlet, they should at least have proper motor transportation facilities towards the Pacific coast. When we found out we could get no assistance whatsoever from any government, regardless of promises in the past, the people of that country got tired and fed up waiting for the fulfilment of promises, and they themselves proceeded to cut through the wilderness and the virgin land of that country a highway which would meet the existing highway system, commencing at Hansard, in British Columbia. So it was that last year hundreds of individuals throughout the Peace River country, of their own accord and by public subscription, cut through fifty-five miles of bush, as a first step towards fulfilling the demand for an outlet from the Peace River country.
I mentioned the circumstances to the minister last year, and I felt this year that under the same measure some financial assistance might be given to help the project along.

He knows as well as I do that the Peace River country is undoubtedly the last great empire in western Canada. Such things as crop failures are unknown in that country, and the only difficulties we encounter are from frost, which lowers the grade of our product. We have never yet had to ask for the expenditure of money because of drought or anything of that kind. I am thankful that it should be so. A population of 65,000 or 70,000 people is certainly entitled to some consideration. The minister knows there is no outlet from the Peace River district to the Pacific coast, and I suggest that moneys spent in carrying out the project to provide a route to the Pacific would help unemployment and agricultural distress.
I understand that at the present time the government is supporting a project to build a highway, known as the Turgeon route-or possibly some other name-to the Pacific coast. It is my further belief that funds for this purpose are being provided by the Department of Mines and Resources with a view to assisting mining development in that part of the country. I understand the hon. member for Cariboo is enthusiastically supporting that project. May I point out to the minister, however, that no more than five per cent of the people in that part of the country could have any possible use for that type of route. I should like to point out, further, that the people of Prince George, which is in the southern part of the Peace River block, and within the constituency of Cariboo, are one hundred per cent in favour of the route proposed by the settlers in the Peace River district, and recently have joined with those settlers and have organized a Monkman pass highway association. I believe this must prove to the hon. member for Cariboo that they desire an outlet to the Pacific coast and not a trail which will help the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company to develop their interests in that country, to the detriment of the 65,000 or 70,000 people living in the district.
I know the minister is busy, but I should like to have him pay some particular attention to the project I have indicated, and to inform himself with respect to it. I mentioned it to him a year ago, but possibly he has not yet had time to go into the details. I hope that he will be able to do so in the near future, and that, of all the governments, out of all the promises, out of all the assurances that have been given, the minister will be the first to make possible an outlet to the Pacific coast from the Peace River country. There are many who would enjoy the benefits of such an outlet. We could obtain fresh fruit

Relief and Agricultural Distress
from British Columbia. We desire to trade with the people of that province. We need what they can supply. But at the present time produce to and from Vancouver must be hauled around by the city of Edmonton. If there were a motor highway from the end of the present highway in Alberta to Hansard, in British Columbia, the Peace River country would benefit immensely. It cannot be said that the project is impossible. Not even a ferry to cross the river is required. The people who started this road built fifty-five miles one year by their free personal contributions without one cent of financial assistance from any government. It is quite a level trail. It would not need any expensive machinery in order to build a decent road, and it is only 155 miles away from a graveled highway in British Columbia. I suggest that it is the minister's duty to pay some heed to the sixty-five or seventy thousand people in the Peace River country who have been located there for many years, who have been promised time and time again that consideration would be given to their demands, but who have not yet received any satisfaction.
I notice that the hon. member for Cariboo is at present in his seat, so I should like to repeat what I said a moment ago concerning the road which it is proposed to build as an outlet for the Peace River country. The people of his constituency, particularly in the region of Prince George, have now formed what is called the Monkman pass highway association to join hands with the Peace River association, and are solidly behind the Monkman project. The other road proposed would benefit only perhaps five per cent of the population of the Peace River country; nevertheless I do not say that the road should not be built. I think we need as much transportation as possible in order to develop our vast national resources. At the same time the most feasible, the quickest and the best way to bring some measure of assistance to the people of the Peace River country is to give the Monkman pass highway association some assistance or for the government to take over the project and provide the Peace River area with that outlet. There is no difficulty in the way; it is an easy route to follow, and it leads to a graveled highway in the northern portion of British Columbia. In this manner an outlet to British Columbia could be provided for the people of the Peace River country in a very short time.

Before we go further, I should like to give some information which I have obtained in reply to the question asked by the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Barber) relating to the operation of the Dominion Housing Act in British Columbia. He was rather critical. I take it, that certain of the lending institutions who operate under agreement with the government under the terms of the Dominion Housing Act were not active in British Columbia.
I think I should say, in fairness to all those who have entered into agreements under the Dominion Housing Act, that what might be called the larger institutions of Canada, both insurance companies and other forms of lending institutions, have dealt far more widely with loans under the Dominion Housing Act than have those localized lending institutions, trust companies and the like, which we find throughout the dominion. In fact, it may very well be said that the larger institutions operating all over Canada are performing a much wider and much more useful service under the Dominion Housing Act than these localized institutions which one would think would be more ready to enter into agreements to meet their own local needs, being so much more familiar with those local needs and being so much closer to the people. That criticism is one not merely of British Columbia institutions; the situation is characteristic of the more localized institutions the dominion over.

speechtext: The hon. member for New Westminster says that those companies are discriminating against some towns.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
I shall make inquiries, of course, with respect to those allegations; but I can say that British Columbia is now well in the van with respect to the number of housing units provided for by loans under the housing act. I got the April report just now, and I find that eighty-six units were approved for loans in British Columbia during that month, bringing the total in that province up to 593 units as at the end of April, 1938. Judging from the amount of prospective business reported through the housing branch of the finance department, British Columbia is taking advantage to an ever-increasing degree of the provisions of the Dominion Housing Act. One must remember, however, that the lender is investing sixty per cent of his own money or the money of his institution, or the trust moneys he is administering, and the department is in no position nor does the act give the minister power to compel any lending institution to lend in any particular locality or to lend on any particular housing security, but every effort is made under the auspices of the housing branch to thresh out problems which arise by reason of allegations that certain municipalities are blacklisted or that loans will not be made to certain areas. We en-

Relief and Agricultural Distress
deavour to take the matter up with the companies most likely to be concerned, and if one does not see its way clear to make loans in a locality we endeavour, through approaches to others who may be interested, to meet the need. It is not always possible to do so, I would advise my hon. friend. There are some municipalities in which the current tax situation, the assessment situation, the financial situation of the municipality, are such as to cause lenders to hesitate in making loans because, even with the dominion proportion, they consider the element of risk too great. We can never get completely away from that difficulty. But the Dominion Housing Act is gradually coming into ever-increasing use with every month which passes. In the two years of active administration of the law some fifteen million dollars worth of housing has been authorized under the act.
In reply to the criticism that it applies only to the higher cost houses, I would point out that 'the average loan per unit is down to something in the neighbourhood of $4,200, and it is constantly coming down as the housing act is being used for an ever-increasing number of lower cost houses. I admit, of course, that there is a field of housing which the Dominion Housing Act cannot possibly meet. Mention has been made during this discussion of the man who has not the twenty per cent to invest in the house in order to provide him with that initial equity, the balance being provided by the lending institution supplemented by the dominion government. In my view that is a separate problem. The low cost housing problem as ieveloped in the report of the employment commission is much more largely a problem of low rental housing than it is a problem of low cost homes to be owned by the inmates of the homes. However, there will be a later occasion to develop that.
The government is not unmindful of the fact that the present legislation does require supplementing. I do not say that it requires change. speechtext:
Yes. It is quite clear
that under present economic conditions the government is not in a position to undertake a rail outlet. At least that is the view which has been expressed by members of the administration, and I believe it is not an unsound one. Certainly during the years from 1930 to 1935 there was no possibility of money being found for that purpose. But there is no reason why a decent highway should not be provided, having regard to the number of people who are without opportunity to get to the coast, and who certainly cannot reach the Atlantic coast and the prairie communities under any reasonable conditions. There has been a rough survey made of what is known as the Monkman pass location extending over

Relief and Agricultural Distress
a distance of about 131 miles from Rio Grande to Hansard. That is Rio Grande in Canada, not the Rio Grande between Mexico and Texas. It would cost a substantial sum of money to make that into a passable highway. But I really think that the people who have made their home there and carried on development and made an annual contribution to our national wealth very large in proportion to their numbers, should have some way of getting out.
I think I could indicate from the records that we do incur some substantial responsibility when we permit people to locate in such areas and build up communities. That has been so in this case. The number of people, given as sixty to seventy thousand, is a little larger than I expected, but I am told that they are actually dependent upon some form of vehicular transportation other than by. rail or water for the purpose of getting to the coast. They cannot get out by our merely giving some little assistance to open up a mining claim or connect them with some locality a few miles distant, because they are scattered over what is known as the Peace River area, and there is no way I can conceive of from my investigation by which they can market their products except by coming down to Rio Grande and from there a distance of 131 miles to a place called Hansard. There are no large streams to bridge, no great difficulties to overcome. I am speaking now from the reports which were received, which may or may not be wholly accurate; it may be that a survey has been made since.

I say to the minister frankly that had the late government had the opportunity with improving revenues, provision would have been made by highway to give these settlers an outlet to the coast, until such time as it became possible to construct a railway. How much time will elapse before that is possible, I do not know.

This would be a reconnaissance, and it indicated that the task of constructing a road would not be too difficult.
The second point to which I wish to direct attention arises out of observations made by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid). I confess I am sensitive upon that question and perhaps I indicated it too readily. The truth is that when we made agreements with the provinces we did not make them with the municipalities, and we insisted on three- not one, or two, but three-methods being followed to protect the exchequer. This had never been done before. I think it is still continued. They were: (1) The certificate of the municipality or spending authority; (2) the province had to give its certificate or there was no money payable; and (3) we insisted on the auditor general making a pre-audit before a dollar was paid. I was able to produce in this chamber original documents showing the method pursued with respect to pre-audit by the auditor general, stamped with the initials of an official of his department, and the comptroller of the treasury informed me definitely that no cheque issued in any case unless and until those prerequisites had been observed.

The circumstances to which the hon. member for New Westminster has referred are in part responsible for that. It did not all arise under one administration either; it was apparently a definite effort on the part of some persons to obtain money and use it for purposes that were not authorized, and notwithstanding that certificates were given they were given without an analysis of the figures to the extent that was proper.
The last point to which I wish to direct the attention of the minister is this: Section 3 with which we are now dealing contemplates the expenditure of large sums of money. I think the minister should give us some indication of how these moneys are to 'be expended, at least more than is indicated in the section itself. I think the committee is entitled to some explanation as to how these moneys are to be utilized. All that is said at the moment is:

may authorize the performance of such acts and the execution of such agreements and contracts as the governor in council may deem necessary and expedient.
Then follows a provision with respect to the utilization of the services of those who are on relief. I have a large volume of correspondence directed to the fact that patronage has become almost an intolerable evil with respect to these expenditures. I have had sufficient experience to appreciate and realize the difficulties that the minister has to meet, and it was for that reason that I welcomed so warmly the Statement made the other day by the Prime Minister with respect to public expenditures. If these were normal times; if the buoyant revenues were being obtained by slight taxation instead of taxation as heavy as in most countries-notwithstanding what may be said, we have a multiplicity of taxing authorities and the aggregate of taxation, direct and indirect, upon the individual in Canada is very heavy-conditions might be different. It is unfair to say that those who contribute largely shall have their money used for the purpose of providing employment for their political opponents, while their friends are debarred from thus being employed. There is no adequate answer that can be made to that argument, and I therefore applauded the observations made the other day by the Prime Minister.

speechtext: It is gratifying to me to hear the remarks that have just been made by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers). But the remarks I am making now are applicable to the legislation before us, which is designed to alleviate agricultural distress and relieve unemployment. The people of that part of Canada look forward to the day when their dream of a railway outlet to the Pacific coast will be realized, and in that connection I might say that I have brought down to the chamber resolutions passed by various boards of trade, particularly the Peace River board

of trade, the whole tenor of which is this: After a great many "whereases," if I may use the phraseology of the hon. member for Comox-Albemi (Mr. Neill), here is one resolution which says:
Be it further resolved that it is now high time that our parliament be advised that Vancouver is not the only spot on our Pacific shore at which an ocean liner can dock, and that the people of the north are quite impatient of being told there is no money for our enterprise while we watch the slow conversion of Montreal into the Jerusalem of Canada with its jasper walls, pearly gates, streets of gold and transparent glass, and the shores of that hallowed St. Lawrence being paved with gold bricks from this New Jerusalem to the sea.
Similar resolutions have been passed by various boards of trade in the Peace River country, and once more I want it clearly understood that the remarks I am going to make regarding the Monkman pass highway association in no way alter my position in regard to the need for a railway outlet to the Pacific coast.
I would point out to the Minister of Labour that the leader of the Liberal party is definitely committed to providing the Peace River country with a railway outlet to the Pacific coast. I have in my hand a report of a speech made in Vancouver by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), dated as far back as July 8, 1930, in which he says that the construction of an outlet from the Peace River district might furnish employment for many now out of work. So, as far back as 1930, the minister's own leader was under the impression that an outlet to the Pacific coast might furnish employment for many now out of work. I realize that the present Minister of Labour may not be fully acquainted with what has taken place in the past concerning an outlet from the Peace River country to the Pacific coast, but I may tell him that the Prime Minister is very well acquainted with the various projects that have been discussed from time to time, and I feel sure that the minister, after consulting with the Prime Minister, should be in a position to give us a definite statement as to what our people in the Peace River country may expect.	_	_
With reference to the highway which it is now proposed should be built, I mentioned the matter to the minister as long ago as last year, when Bill N"o. 80 was under discussion. Perhaps the minister has not all the information before him, so in order to make sure that the information is laid before the committee and that the minister may know what the people of that part of the country want, I have, brought with me a fairly large map showing the proposed outlet.

Relief and Agricultural Distress
This is a map of that part of the Peace River block which shows the need of the present highway in British Columbia, in the northern part of the province, and also shows the highway which comes from the southern part of British Columbia and runs as far north as Hansard, in that province, on the Canadian National railway. The gap to be built is a stretch of 132 miles between Rio Grande on the north and Hansard on the south. The construction of the road does not present any difficulties. People have already been over that road many times in wagons, and as the leader of the opposition said, it is not a question of attempting any engineering feats. It is quite easy to build the road, and I should be very happy to offer this map to the minister on behalf of the people of the Peace River country so that he will be in a position to know exactly what we in that part of the country desire.
Last year, when Bill No. 80 was under discussion, we were given no more idea of what was going to be done for unemployment than we are being given to-day, but supplementary estimates were later brought down and by item 302 the sum of $7,331,000 was appropriated as a federal contribution to provincial and municipal relief projects. That was only part of the moneys which were spent, and as the minister said this afternoon, not a single dollar of that was spent, I believe, to assist in the construction of an outlet from the Peace River country. It is true that the government has supplied some moneys for what will eventually become an outlet. I have before me a sketch of the proposed highway to which the present federal government has been contributing in some degree through the Minister of Mines and Resources. I believe it is called the Turgeon route. Instead of going eastward from Prince George, it goes westward and from Manson creek north to Finlay Forks, and then swings to the east to Hudson Hope. The proposed route, on which moneys are already being expended, is 600 miles long, but you know, Mr. Chairman, just as well as I do, how long it will take to build 600 miles if we are going to build only from thirty to forty miles each year as a measure to assist in giving employment.
I repeat that all those who are interested in the development of the Peace River country, no matter where they live, realize that the best and shortest route to give us an immediate and direct outlet from the Peace River country is the so-called Monkman pass highway. It is needless to go over the arguments that have already been presented, but I should like to point out that nowhere else
have people had the courage to get up and do the work of road building themselves when no government funds were coming from any quarter. The people themselves went about the country collecting food, money, axes and equipment; they volunteered to work and volunteered the use of equipment, and then of their own accord they got busy and began to build an outlet to the Pacific coast because the people of the Peace River country are determined that eventually we are going to enjoy the benefits of being able to trade with British Columbia. There is not a member of this committee who comes from that province who does not desire to see this project brought to a successful conclusion. Why? Simply because we in the northern part of Alberta, offer a market for the fresh fruits and garden: stuff of British Columbia, which is at present closed to us. To-day it is impossible for us to bring in these fruits and other products over the present route. We have to ship the stuff from Vancouver around by Edmonton or Calgary and then north again four hundred miles to the Peace River country, and all we need is a highway 132 miles long to give sixty-five to seventy thousand people the advantages which such an outlet would confer upon the Peace River country.
In addition to these arguments I should-mention that for several weeks past I have been receiving a large volume of correspondence from that section of the Peace River country. Letters have poured in from the Peace River block in British Columbia. All the residents in the Peace River areas in British Columbia and Alberta are united in their desire to have an outlet to the Pacific coast. They hope that before long the Monk-man pass highway will be an accomplished fact. I repeat that it is the most direct and the best outlet at the present time. It is not a matter of expending millions of dollars,", we are not talking in millions. We are content -at times-to let other portions of Canada, get the millions if we can obtain only a few thousands. W e have waited long and up to the present we have waited in vain. The people in that particular part of Canada are not people to whom only one provincial * government can be held to be responsible. As the leader of the opposition said this afternoon, the settlement in that particular part of f the country is made up of people who come1 from eastern Canada and of French Canadians-who left the industrial centres in the eastern United States to come west and settle this land. The country produces each year upwards of twenty million bushels of wheat..

Relief and Agricultural Distress
It is exporting all kinds of products, and it certainly deserves consideration by this committee and particularly by the Minister of Lalbour -when he makes out his list of moneys to 'be voted to help the provinces in respect of unemployment relief. At a later date I hope to -be in a position to thank the minister sincerely for having listened to our earnest pleas and given us some assistance. If he does so he will be, as I have remarked before, the first man in Canada to recognize the needs of that area of the Peace River country; and I am sure that, regardless of our views on other matters, we shall all be grateful to him. After all, all we seek is a little justice.

This particular newspaper article which calls this route the Turgeon highway has this to say. They are advocating the Monkman pass and the writer says "Unfortunately, Mr. Turgeon, the member for the district, is committed to this other route." He makes this proposal-and I have in mind what the hon. gentleman just said in the

Relief and Agricultural Distress
closing words of his remarks to which I shall refer again: If only we could have Mr. Turgeon support the Monkman pass and make a deal with the Prime Minister of Canada, and relieve the Prime Minister of Canada of his obligation and the obligation of all political parties to build a railroad into Peace River and substitute the Monkman pass, then, we would all be satisfied.
The hon. member must have read during the dinner hour a resolution prepared by the people of Peace River town, or Peace River Crossing as we used to call it in the old days in Alberta, which town is in the hon. gentleman's riding. According to that resolution the people there are not enthusiastically supporting the construction which he is asking for to-night. There are different ports on the Pacific; there is Vancouver, there is Prince Rupert, and there is Stewart; and the people of the Peace River district

I am referring now not to the riding generally, but to Peace River Crossing, or town-are rather inclined to favour construction through the Peace pass on to Stewart or to Prince Rupert. Just within the last few weeks they passed a resolution to that effect. While the hon. gentleman did not say so, I rather think that is the resolution which he is now reading in order that the people of the north country, having read all the other speeches he has made to-day and on other occasions with respect to this matter, will not think he is neglecting them altogether, will not think he is forgetting about the length of time that the people of the Peace River district have asked for a railroad into that country. And so he comes here to-night and reads us what I fancy-I may be wrong and he will correct me if I am-is an extract from a resolution passed by the board of trade of Peace River Crossing in his constituency.
Several things must be borne in mind when one is talking to this government-and when I say " this government," I mean the government of Canada-in connection with the construction of any highway, whether from the Peace River area or not. One of them is that up to this very hour all works of this kind have been done jointly by the dominion and the province involved. The dominion could not say to the province, " We want to build a road here and we will not give you our money if you want to build it in another place." The works had to :be done jointly or they would not have been done at all. What was done was done on the strength given to the Dominion of Canada by the new mining policy initiated by this government now in office under the prime ministership of the right hon. gentleman whose words the hon.

member for Peace River quoted to-night and quoted in the speech he made a year ago, trying to throw something back into the right hon. gentleman's face. The pledge he quoted, which was made some years back, was for the construction of a railway from the Peace River district to the coast. This government, having in mind not necessarily pledges but the necessities of the people of that northern country, were glad to aid the province of British Columbia in the development of the project which they wished to push out from Fort St. James towards Manson creek and which might run to Finlay Forks, and one result of that road work, leaving out altogether if you wish what it might mean to the people of the Peace River district, was that, while up to and including the first part of the mining season of 1936 the largest number of men ever employed in that whole Omineca area by private industry in the search for gold was about seventy-five, certainly not more than one hundred, last year, only twelve months after the commencement of work, the number of men employed by private industry had increased from under one hundred to over six hundred. Is that not something for the Minister of Labour to be proud of? Is that something which must be held up against him in this house and it be said that the government of which he is a member are doing this only for the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company?
Let me tell the committee something more. We have running through the province of British Columbia what is called the Pacific Great Eastern railway. I think every hon. member has heard of that railway. In years past the Alberta government-I remember this well because later on I was a member of the Alberta legislature-voted money towards the instruction of the railway called the Edmonton, Dunvegan and British Columbia railway, the intention of the Alberta legislators being to have that railway extended through the province of British Columbia to the coast. But the Pacific Great Eastern was constructed, or partly constructed, in British Columbia, and for years the dream has been cherished that eventually these two railway lines would be connected. From that several results would follow. The people of the Peace River district both in Alberta and in British Columbia would obtain that outlet which they have so earnestly desired for many years; and the province of British Columbia would be relieved of the burden resting upon it by reason of the fact that the Pacific Great Eastern, while doing excellent work in the small area which it serves, is not on a paying basis owing to the smallness of that area.

Relief and Agricultural Distress
Is 'there anything that would do more to bring about the construction of a railway in the future than the development of the natural resources of the country through which that railway would run? What are the natural resources of that country? The right hon. leader of the opposition to-day mentioned an engineering survey made some years ago by a commission consisting of a representative of each railway, the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific, and a representative of the provincial government who was the chairman. I have here a summary of statements prepared by the chairman of that commission. I shall not weary the committee by reading much of this, but he advises that of all the passes observed by the commission and their employees the one most suitable for the construction of a highway is that from Prince George almost directly north and a little west, down the waterways which commence thirty-five miles north of Prince George at Summit lake, to Pinlay Forks and down the Peace river as far as you might have to go. I found it impossible to secure money directly to build a highway into the Peace River block, so as the member for that district I did the next best thing that was possible, helped to bring about the development of some of the natural resources which the chairman of that engineering commission told me would unquestionably be found in that country. And that mining development in Omineca of which I have told the committee is simply a demonstration of the foresight displayed by the chairman of that commission away back in 1934 when he made his recommendation to me. His report stated:
The bulk of the timber and mineral resources will be directly tributary to this route and the largest area of agricultural lands, in the lower Parsnip and Finlay valleys and north of the Peace river in British Columbia, will also be best served by this location of the highway. This highway will afford access to 2,800,000 acres of cultivable lands largely suitable for mixed farming, 6,862,000 thousand board feet of merchantable timber, 4,800,000 cords of pulp-wood, and 7,000 square miles of mineralized areas, especially deposits estimated of over 600,000,000 tons of semi-anthracite and semibituminous coal.
