No; that is another coal bed entirely, mainly along Carbon creek, but along the Peace river generally. That coal has been analyzed here at Ottawa and it tests ash free. There is a market for that. If we can produce in Canada anthracite coal which the government analysts find ash free we have a market for it, especially when running right through that coal bed is one of the greatest undeveloped water powers in Canada. There is running through that coal area twelve to fourteen miles of canyon through which the Peace river rushes with all its force. And right alongside of it-although I am not quite so sure of this as I am of the other resources-is evidence of iron ore. You have your coal and your water power and the possibility of iron ore all within the same area. And right on up the river you have gold and base metals. Just beyond the junction of the three great streams, the Parsnip river, running northeast, the Finlay river running southwest and the Peace river, which is gouged out of the rocks by the other two streams, you find your gold in the Omineca country, which I described a little while ago.
The hon. member for Peace River said that the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company are interested in this north country. Of course they are. I am inclined to think that for many years that great corporation, like other large corporations, was not anxious that the great potential value of that area should be known. I do not blame them for that because they wanted to develop that country quietly on their own. They were not demanding the building of roads at that time, and it was only after we started a road and other companies came in and began to find gold in paying quantities that the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company made a request for that road. Prior to the time that I had a recommendation made through the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie), the minister from British Columbia in this government; prior to the time that a recommendation for the construction of the road was made to the government and accepted, the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company had never said one word to me, orally or by letter, asking for the building of that road. Since then they have and they have been anxious to have it continued. I am glad that the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company are there.
It will be remembered that in the session of 1936 applications were made by the two railway companies to obtain permission to build a railroad into the Rouyn district of

Reliej and Agricultural Distress
northern Quebec. As the hon. gentleman behind me knows, the people in that district had been trying for years without success, perhaps as long as the people in the Peace River district, to obtain transportation facilities. As soon as it was shown that there were mining possibilities in the section, there was no more difficulty in obtaining the construction of a railroad. Both railway companies were anxious to build and vied with each other for the privilege of serving the people in the Rouyn district. Although I have nothing upon which to base a hope, I am hoping that before long one of the great railway companies, at least the one that is directly interested in the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company, will see its way clear to commence negotiations for the acquisition of the Pacific Great Eastern railway and its extension into the Peace River district. My hope is based upon the success which has attended the efforts of this government to develop that northern country.
While this roadwork has been going on, another thing has taken place. I mentioned the Canadian National Railways branch from Jasper to Prince Rupert. That branch has always run in the red; it is still running in the red; but its operating income has increased very materially in the last two years due to the mining operations that have taken place in the Omineca country following the expenditure of these few thousands of dollars. I know that the leaders in the Monkman pass association will not thank the hon. member for Peace River for the manner in which he has brought this matter to the attention of the committee. I know the hon. member is a member of that association, of which I had the honour of becoming a member in the last thirty days.
I am proud to be a member of that association and I want to compliment its members upon the way they have gone about their work. However, I do not think I need tell hon. members that there are other men and women in other areas who should be considered. Let us deal in facts. A road cannot be built into the Peace River country for a few thousand dollars. Such a thing is utterly impossible. To build a highway through the Monkman pass or by any other route will cost over a million dollars. It is easy to say there are no bridges to be built, but how are you going to cross the Fraser and some of the other rivers? The same thing is true of the other routes, which will cost more than the Monkman route. The Monkman pass route cannot be built for less than a million dollars.
I do not want to detain the committee any longer except to say that I am not opposed

to the construction of the Monkman pass highway if funds can be secured. However, I am most bitterly opposed to those who are throwing cold water upon the efforts of this government based upon the recommendations, largely of myself and the minister from British Columbia, to develop the resources of the north country. I ask the hon. member for Peace River, as I asked those who are concerned directly with the association organized to bring about the construction of the Monkman pass road: In order to make certain that you have a short route over which automobiles can travel from the grain growing section of the Peace River district of Alberta to the Cariboo highway, are you going to sacrifice the interests of those people who live contiguous to the Peace river? Are you going to sacrifice the interests of nine-tenths of the people in the Peace River block of British Columbia who want another outlet and who want their country developed? What are you going to do with the people at Fort St. John and Hudson Hope? What are you going to do with the people who live all along the Peace river?
It has been said that a road by any route other than the Monkman pass would be longer. Last year the hon. member said it would be six hundred miles longer, but that is just a flight of his imagination. It is not anything like six hundred miles in its entire length, let alone being six hundred miles longer than any other route. The people at Fort St. John are just as much entitled to an outlet as the people at Grande Prairie, and I say this without having anything against the people in that community. When you are estimating distances, where should they be estimated from? Why choose Grande Prairie rather than Fort St. John? Why choose Grande Prairie rather than Hudson Hope? Why choose one point rather than another? If you are estimating the distance from an area to an important point, say Vancouver or Prince Rupert, you must take some central point in the area.

speechtext: As I understand it, it was not proposed that this would be a solution of the transportation difficulty. It provided only a temporary outlet for a given population in a given area. My support was directed to it entirely on that assumption.

speechtext:
I appreciate that. I am glad the right hon. gentleman mentioned that and, with his permission, I should like to ask a question. He has had serious responsibilities placed upon him. For five years he was Prime Minister of this country, and he knows, of course, of the crying need and the

Relief and, Agricultural Distress
necessity for an outlet of some kind for the people of the Peace River country. I would ask the right hon. gentleman this question: If without further consideration a government of which he was the head built a highway over the Monkman pass, would there be any use whatever for myself or anybody else to go to his government again and ask for another outlet from the Peace River to the coast? There would not be. That is the trouble.
I fully recognize and appreciate the feelings of the right hon. gentleman in this regard. Of course it is all right to say that this is just a temporary thing; it is all right to say that the idea is to give them an outlet, but the minute we give the people of the Peace River country one outlet they will never get another. There is no question about that. Therefore we must be careful in our decision os to what outlet we may give them. Therefore I say it is the supreme duty of the government concerned with that project, and especially the minister from British Columbia, to do just what he has been doing, namely to help in the development of the natural resources of that great north country. I know the people in that area have given a great deal. As I have pointed out to the Prime Minister and to other ministers, they have given so much that they have almost lost faith in the institution of government. I have asked this government-and to a limited extent they have acceded to my request-to do something not only for Omineca pass, but for the whole outlet, so that the thousands of people who live in the north country will regain their faith in man and in the institution of government. I have asked for that, and I hope their day is coming.
I was about to say, when the right hon. gentleman asked his question, that within the next few weeks-if they have not already started-a company will be drilling for oil in the Peace River district in Alberta, right outside the British Columbia town of Pouce Coupe. I am inclined to think they will be successful and will secure oil and gas-certainly gas, if not oil. If that takes place, all the conditions surrounding the question of Monkman pass will have changed. If those resources are found, a great natural resource will have been discovered, one which would be well worth tapping. But even if they do not succeed there are, in addition to the other natural material resources I mentioned, two known structures where, according to geologists, oil and gas are most likely to be found. Those structures have never been touched, and nobody knows actually whether
or not oil and gas are there. Geologists go so far as to say that they are. These two gas and oil structures are in the south western portion of the Peace River block, contiguous again to Hudson Hope.
It is not my fault if most of those natural resources, other than cattle and grain, are in that part of the Peace River district. I did not put them there. I am simply trying to bring to the attention of the committee the fact that they are there, and to see that whatever can be done by governments is done, so that those resources may be properly developed. That is all I am trying to do, and that is all that need be done. As I pointed out in the beginning, almost every dollar spent in the construction of the Monk-man pass highway, if undertaken, and every other highway in that section of the country, would be over my constituency.
I have been in the house for a long time. Before making his attack last year, certainly before making it to-day, and before trying to tie it up with the requirements and the necessities of a great mining company, I suggest the hon. member might have spoken to me, and ascertained whether or not we could get together. If what he had in mind was not a grievance against the government but simply the desire for construction, and if that desire could have been accomplished by a thorough knowledge of conditions, then I suggest the hon. member should have discussed the matter with me with a view to seeing whether or not we could get together and give relief to the people in the Rio Grande valley, Grande Prairie and in other parts of the Peace River district of Alberta. He should have ascertained whether or not by getting together we could help to get them the relief of which they are deserving, just as deserving as the people in the Omineca country, at Finlay Forks or at Hudson Hope.
I take my seat now in the hope that acrimony will be dissipated; that all bitterness may be dispelled, and that this government will continue to develop the resources and make surveys such as I have requested them to make. I have requested that the mining road through the Omineca country be continued, and that in the meantime a thorough observational survey, having regard to the natural resources, and all matters to which consideration should be given, be made. I do not refer to a survey costing thousands of dollars. My request is for an observational survey which would be done in addition to developing the natural resources of the country. The best route would be decided upon, and then this government and the government of British Columbia, if they worked

Relief and Agricultural Distress
together-if they do not work together this government should proceed to provide the necessary expenditure of between one and two million dollars-could build that highway out of the Peace River district to the settled portions of British Columbia, thereby giving the district the transportation system it deserves.

We have had a long discussion on the Peace River outlet, and while I am very much interested in the Peace River country and the building of a road through Monkman pass, and in many other matters discussed by the two previous speakers, the unemployment problem, extending as it does from the Atlantic to the Pacific, is, I think, a little larger than the question of the Peace River country.
The reason I wish to say a word or two is that the minister seems to have developed in the last session or two, a very wise habit of saying as little as possible, which is an exceedingly prudent attitude for a minister who is trying to get his legislation through the house to adopt. But we are thirsting for information. While the newspapers seem to be able sometimes to make intelligent guesses as to the intentions of the government along certain lines, we in the house are unable to obtain any information whatsoever. For some time past it has been stated in the press, for example, that the government intends spending $40,000,000 on public works projects. I do not know whether that is correct or not, and while the minister may inform the committee that the proper time to discuss that aspect of the question is when the estimates are before the committee of supply, I think when we are discussing unemployment and the methods to be adopted for relieving it we might well have a statement from the minister in regard to the policy of the government. It is all very well for the minister to inform the committee that he is following precedent or the action of the previous government, but really I do not think the present government ought to follow in the footsteps of its predecessor because we well remember what happened to the previous government in 1935. So I should think it was a risky policy when the policy of the present government follows exactly the course taken by the previous one. I should like this government to go the previous government one better. I would ask the minister to state frankly to the committee what program the government has in view for dealing with this problem of unemployment.
I think it is well to point out to the committee that this unemployment problem has been with us for the past eight years, during which time we have had three governments in power. In 1929 we had the commencement of what we might call the unemployment situation which is still with us. In 1930 the present government dissolved1 parliament, and we know what the result of the election of

1930 was. Another government came into power and stayed in power until 1935. Then, from 1935 to 1938 we have had another government in power, and yet the position in regard to unemployment is exactly the same to-day, in 1938, as it was in 1930. In other words, I would ask the Minister of Labour and the Prime Minister if we have made any progress towards solving the problem of unemployment when we are still doing in 1938 what we were doing in 1930 and onwards. They have recognized the
problem and are doing something about it, I admit, but what they are doing is training youth for positions that do not exist. That is the important point.
I am anxious for the government to leave the old methods that we have followed for a number of years and to do something more fundamental and constructive. I have been urging that upon the government now for a number of years. While I acquiesce in the policy of relief and in the policy of building public works to alleviate the unemployment situation, I think everybody in the house is agreed that neither of these two methods of dealing with the unemployment problem is in any way a solution of it.
I wish hon. members would speak as frankly and openly in the house as they do when they speak privately. I am not directing my remarks at anyone in particular. The hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deach-man) said this afternoon that he would like the government to come out with a definite policy for meeting the unemployment situation, but evidently the government are not anxious or are not in a position to do so. Possibly they have no policy.
I think when we are discussing in this chamber this problem of unemployment and its implications, we sometimes treat the whole question a little too lightly. We have unemployed in this country to-day to the number, I believe, of 400,000, and if that is
the case-and I do not believe I am overstating it-it is a tremendous problem from the standpoint of the industrial population. When this government came into power in 1935 they came into power on what one might call a rising tide of industrial recovery. We were in a period of improving times, just as in 1930 industrial production was on the decline. This matter cuts right across government activities because, if you take the last few years, we find that when the government left office in 1930 we were in a decline so far as industrial production was concerned, which decline continued until we reached the bottom, about 1932, and from 1932 or 1933 until 1937 we were on a rising tide of industrial recovery, with improvement continuing all those years. In 1937 we again reached probably the peak of industrial development, and we are now on the decline again.
Are we going to say in this house that we are going to be dependent upon what is done in the United States? Are we going to be told that if the United States spends a few more billions of dollars we in Canada may reap some benefit from what is being done in other parts of the world; that if Great Britain spends billions of dollars for armaments, some of which may be manufactured in this country, we may derive some benefit from her expenditures? Do you not think, Mr. Chairman, that the right and logical thing for us to do in this country is for the government to give us a policy of its own, distinct and apart altogether from anything that is being done by any other government outside this dominion? I am anxiously looking for the government to give its policy to the house. It was all right when they came into office in 1935, in a period of expanding trade, to say: We will depend upon foreign markets and trade treaties to improve economic conditions in this dominion. But now the position is reversed; we are in a decline, and I would ask the government at this stage to come forward and give us a definite policy of what they are going to do in regard to the whole unemployment situation. I think it is most unsatisfactory, after we have had an unemployment problem for eight years, still to think in the eighth year of the depression that we are going to cure unemployment by giving relief to those who are out of work and occasionally providing a scheme of public works projects, such as public buildings, and so forth.
The minister told us this afternoon, if I heard him correctly, that so far as public works projects, were concerned, what the government had in mind was public works projects having to do with conservation.

Has the government done anything to modernize or to extend the Employment Service of Canada? In reading the report of the national employment commission I was struck by the emphasis they place on the need for a better employment service in Canada. Apparently that is also the viewpoint of the different provinces. The report shows further that the commission have been stressing this need with the government ever since August, 1936. In the interim report dated July 21, 1937, we find at page 17 these words:
Early in the commission's investigation it became evident that the first and most vital step necessary to the successful handling of employment, re-employment and aid administration problems is the development of more efficient employment services throughout Canada. The present provincial employment services are in practice unfitted to meet the exigencies of the situation.
Then we find in the final report made in January of this year that even stronger language is used at page 15 dealing with the machinery to carry out recommendations summarized in the interim report:
The requirement here, as pointed out on page 19 of the interim report, is the prompt modernization and extension of the Employment Service of Canada, this with a view to
a better linking together of employer and employee; to providing focal points for attacks on local employment problems, and as a means of gauging the relative degree of employability of those in receipt of aid. In discussions which the commission has had in recent months, general agreement has been expressed by all provincial governments-
Which seems strange.
-as to the unsuitability of the existing set-up, and of the restricted services, of the provincial employment services in fulfilling these vital functions.
My understanding is that the provincial governments operate the service, but they are subsidized by the dominion.
Then the recommendation goes on:
The commission wishes to emphasize the urgency for action. It recommends that the service be placed immediately under the direction of the dominion government, both as to controlling principles and broad policies, but with provision for the appointment of strong regional directors, and regional advisory councils, to whom certain decentralized powers would be given, so as to ensure adequate weight being accorded, and attention being paid, to the problems peculiar to particular regions. The success of any nation-wide program of local plans developed in order to disperse the remaining problem is undoubtedly dependent upon such reorganization.
I understood from what the minister said, in discussing the resolution which preceded this bill, that he was not prepared to accept this recommendation at the present time. Would it not be possible, at least, to improve the situation at the present time by arranging with the provinces for these advisory committees to be set up in each province to aid the provincial employment agencies, and would it not be possible also to strengthen the employment agencies by a larger subsidy from the dominion? It does seem to me that there is need for better employment agencies in Canada. Surely this government could do something at the present time to meet the need at least in part.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
This question of the Employment Service of Canada is one that has been discussed before in this chamber. As my hon. friend may recall, I dealt with it at some length during the discussion of the resolution preceding the bill. The national employment commission did recommend that the Employment Service of Canada should be brought under national direction and control, and the suggestion was that by being so brought under national direction and control that service would be improved and modernized. I did not hesitate to say to the house some time ago that I fully agreed with the desirability of improving the Employment Service of Canada, but that I did not agree

Relief and Agricultural Distress
it was desirable that that service should be taken over piecemeal; in other words, I did not believe that it would serve to create efficiency in the employment service, having regard to the task confronting it, to take over the employment service in Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, and establish it as a national service in those provinces, leaving the service as it now is in the remaining provinces.
Despite the phrase quoted by my hon. friend a moment ago to the effect that the provincial governments agreed as to the unsuitability of the existing service, I am in a position to say that the provincial governments generally did not agree and do not now agree that the service should be taken over as a dominion service. That is particularly true of the more highly industrialized provinces of the dominion. The provinces that are willing to have the dominion take over the service are the provinces where the service is of the least importance; the provinces that are most unwilling for the dominion to take it over are the more highly industrialized provinces. I did suggest when the matter was under discussion before, and I think it is a correct view, that in the long run it would not be sound policy to have a national employment service in three, or four, or five provinces, and to have the existing system perpetuated in the remaining provinces.
I also mentioned, when the matter was under discussion before, that if and when we were able to proceed with unemployment insurance, the problem would be solved in the most effective way, because through unemployment insurance you have to set up, as a necessary part of the organization, employment offices in all the large centres of population, and those employment offices, by reason of their very continuing relationship with industry, would be in a position to render service superior to that of any provincial service, if, indeed, under those conditions a provincial service would be maintained.
That is the situation with regard to the Employment Service of Canada at the present time. I agree that if we are not able to change the situation immediately, there is much to be said for the improvement and modernization of the service. I am not prepared to say that the provinces, which themselves have expressed the view that the service does need improvement, are not in a position themselves to provide that improvement. In other words, I would not go so far as to say that improvement, particularly in the large industrial provinces, is contingent upon a larger contribution from the dominion government. As a matter of fact, the contribution of the dominion government to the

Employment Service of Canada does not run very much above twenty per cent of the total cost. Our contribution is $150,000 a year. The service is not an expensive one at the present time, and it could be improved in a number of provinces without a very great increase in expenditure.
If I might refer briefly to the points raised by my hon. friend from Winnipeg North, I would assure him and the committee generally that with respect to any program to deal with unemployment, I have given to the press no information which has been withheld from the house. Any stories that have appeared in the press have been speculative. There should not be and there will not be any official announcement of expenditure in relation to unemployment in advance of the submission of the supplementary estimates to the house. My hon. friend may say that I should at this time at least give an outline of what we propose to do in relation to unemployment. I think it not unreasonable to suggest to him that he might read the supplementary estimates of the Department of Labour and of other departments in the two preceding years. He will find there that provision has been made in a number of directions to deal with unemployment and agricultural distress. There have been grants in aid to the provinces. As he has said, that simply provides sustenance during a period of urgent need. There is also provision for works to be done jointly with the provinces. There was provision last year for training projects for unemployed young people, and there has been provision for relief settlement or what might be termed agricultural rehabilitation. There also has been provision in the Department of Agriculture for assistance to farmers in connection with feed and fodder. He will find that in those items in the estimates under the Department of Labour and the Department of Agriculture, regardless of whether the emphasis or the extent of assistance has been as great as he woidd wish, we have at least been proceeding along the lines of proved experience, and we have been touching this problem at the very points where it has been touched by unemployment policies in other countries.
We have lacked here-and I regret it- what exists in other countries, namely, an unemployment insurance statute, which after all enables a country to set up a statutory method and to establish an organization to deal with the problem as it may vary from one area to another or from one period to another. In other words, with unemployment insurance you at least have a flexible organization to deal with what may be a changing

Relief and Agricultural Distress
situation with respect to unemployment. But this government has sought so to arrange its fiscal policies and its assistance to industry in other directions as to assist towards greater collateral and ultimate employment.
I do not wish now to retrace ground I covered during the discussion of the resolution; but I think my hon. friend will at least agree that the policies pursued by this government with respect to the stimulus to the mining industry, and the gaining of foreign markets for our produce, have been policies with which he is in entire accord, and which certainly, in their successful working, have provided additional employment in Canada. There is no question about that; the figures prove it beyond contradiction. So that, although my hon. friend is perfectly entitled to say that we have not done enough in this direction, or perhaps too much in that direction, as far as the policies themselves are concerned, I would be interested to know from him in what other directions we may proceed than expansion of trade, stimulation of private industry, rural rehabilitation, public works on a limited scale, provision through direct relief for those who are actually in need, and, in addition training schemes which we trust will ultimately lead to the reestablishment of many of those in the lower age groups who are now unemployed. These after all are policies which experience has approved, and I submit that criticism should be directed rather to the application of the policies than to their merits.

speechtext: In the light of present day developments, does the minister think the policies which he has outlined, supposing we admit that they have been effective in some measure, touch the fundamentals of the unemployment problem?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
As to what the fundamentals of the unemployment problem are, this house might debate for many days without reaching any common conclusion. I find myself largely in agreement with some things said this afternoon by the hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deachman). If we can employ our fiscal policies in this country so as to lighten the burdens on the agricultural industry particularly, that would be a move in the right direction. I believe something may very usefully be done in the direction of conservation and development works to improve the assets of the country and lead ultimately, one may hope, to greater employment in that direction. Expanding trade, gaining foreign markets through trade agreements, is most certainly a means of providing additional employment. But I shall not
deceive my hon. friend with the thought that as far as I am concerned I have any faith that there is any single solution. I believe we have something to learn in connection with control of credit. No one can reasonably say that with respect to that matter we have learned all that there is to be learned. We are living in a progressive society. But in all these things we must move forward step by step, making sure of our way as we go. There is no single panacea. I have before me the report of the international labour office on unemployment. It relates to all countries which are members of the international labour office, and all of them are suffering from unemployment. I suppose if one took the various devices and plans adopted in all these countries and put them together, it would include every suggestion put forward in this chamber in this and the preceding two years; yet unemployment continues in greater or less measure in these countries. And it must be remembered that in this country there has always been seasonal unemployment. In 1929, when we thought we were at the peak of prosperity, there were about 150,000 people reported by the bureau of statistics as unemployed during the winter months.

Yes; but in 1929 we thought we were prosperous; yet there were about

I think it is true that the people of this country in the lowest income group, taken by and large, are better cared for than they have been at any previous period in our history. We should recognize that. My hon friends may well say that here and there relief allowances are not what they ought to be, but one cannot draw conclusions from individual cases of that kind.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Is that not a strong indictment of the system under which we live?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
Well, I wonder if it is
What is happening is that we have been providing what my hon. friends would term a measure of social security, in an improvised and perhaps haphazard way during the past few years. I am far from suggesting that it is satisfactory; I agree absolutely with what has been said in this chamber, that we ought to look to employment as the real solution.

Relief and Agricultural Distress

But the experience of all the countries, members of the international labour office, does not suggest that we are likely to be able to absorb all who are at present unemployed unless there is a very marked improvement in economic conditions. During the last few years this country has had a large portion of its agricultural area out of production. It is difficult to measure the effect of that upon our economy. I doubt whether we can measure it until that agricultural area has come back into production. When it does, as we all hope it soon will, I believe we shall find that the unemployment properly so-called which now exists in western Canada will be materially reduced, if it does not entirely disappear.
I am now speaking not of unemployables but of those in the larger cities of western Canada who are out of employment. In the last few years the whole economy of western Canada has been thrown out of adjustment by the fact that a large part of the potentially productive area of that section of the country has not been producing.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
The remarks of the hon.
member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Heaps) impel me to offer some contribution in this debate. First, I wish to express my appreciation to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) for his splendid explanation and his defence of his department. I often marvel at his patience and the careful way in which he listens to all the criticisms; he must have a very gracious disposition to take it with such good nature. But it is fitting that he should take this opportunity of defending the department of which he has the honour to be the head.
The remarks and suggestions of the hon. member for Winnipeg North regarding the solution of our problems were extremely interesting. I congratulate him; whether they were sound or otherwise, he did at least to the best of his ability offer suggestions for the approach to these problems. But, as the hon. member for Renfrew North (Mr. Warren) remarked, I do not see how the high level of wages that the hon. member advocates could solve our problems, because after all in Canada the agriculturists are the greatest consuming group. How are you going to harmonize high wages with low cost of goods, so that the purchasing power of the agriculturists will be in reasonable balance with that of industry? These are some of the difficulties we have to face. You cannot have your cake and eat it too. There must be a reasonable exchange of services among the different elements of society. I am inclined to the view that many of our difficulties are traceable to the fact that we have been

giving too large a reward for the labour of those who live in the industrial centres, and thus curtailed the purchasing power of the greatest consumers of their goods in this country. Thereby we have aggravated a situation that has been responsible to a great extent for bringing about the condition of affairs which exists. We have created a magnetic influence upon the farmer boys to attract them into the cities to obtain the higher wages and live under higher standards. All this has been done more or less at the sacrifice of the agricultural industry.
If the Minister of Labour will permit me,
I should like to take this opportunity to offer a suggestion. I do not claim to be an economist in the general sense of the word, but I dio claim to have at least a reasonable amount of common sense. I do not see how it will be possible to accept the many recommendations made by hon. members opposite without finding some source from which these things can oome.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Source of money.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Yes, source of money. I have never been able to get money except ill exchange for services. In my experience of life I have never discovered any other way of getting money. It is true that I may have established a certain amount of credit after living in a community for 'a period of years, but I am sufficiently jealous of that credit to toe anxious about making use of it too elaborately for fear that I may live to reap the whirlwind as a result of my folly.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
I shall not attempt to match wits with hon. members of the social credit group. They might carry me into that state of coma in which they are themselves and I might not come out.
Considerable credit has been given to the government for initiating a youth training program. I hope there have been some results from this program, but I must say that I do not believe it is incumbent upon the state to train the youth of the country. After all, we as parents should have some obligations in the matter. The tendency is to ask governments to do many of the things which I think could be better done by ourselves. I do not want to imply for one moment that I

Relief and Agricultural Distress
am against academic training. Unfortunately I did not have an opportunity of obtaining that particular kind of training, but I have noticed that many of the prominent men in this country and the United States are in a similar position. I would direct attention to the fact that Mr. Farrell, the head, of the United States Steel Corporation, the heads of the Standard Oil companies and many other leaders of industry were poor boys who were raised on the farm. Many of them were not blessed with an abundance of this world's goods and had received only a limited public school education. But they have risen to be masters in their own particular line. I would also direct attention to the fact that many of the members who sit on the ministerial benches have risen to their present positions without the benefit of a great deal of academic training. Even without that training they have been able to come a long way in this world. I do not expect as much from this youth training as others seem to do, but I have no particular objection to it.
I was glad to hear the minister make a reference to unemployment insurance. When that plan is brought down I hope the farmer will be kept in mind, because after all he represents a large portion of the population of Canada. I hope that measure will provide some benefits for the agricultural worker. I do not think the citizens living in our industrial centres should be the only ones who are to be protected from unemployment, who are to be given the means of weathering the storms of our economic difficulties.
I think we must all admit that our attempts to solve the unemployment problem have not been as successful as we hoped they would be. I wonder if it would not be better for the government to subsidize employment instead of unemployment. We are paying out relief funds to those who are in the unfortunate position of being unemployed without getting any value in return. I do not think we can continue to do that without reaching financial disaster. I am inclined to the view that we should subsidize industry. I shall not suggest what this subsidy should be, but for the sake of argument I would suggest that some pump-priming, to use that term, should be done.

I do not know whether that

speechtext:
We shall come to that later.
I can show you how you will get it back. I
believe too much pump-priming of a sort has been done. We have been trying to prime the pump without working the handle, and I think we should start now to work the handle to see if we cannot get back some of the water. During this last year industry has enjoyed a fairly good period of prosperity. Most industries have expanded; but the unfortunate thing is that industry has increased prices and has reduced the purchasing power of the consumer, especially in the United States, to such an extent as to bring about another recession. More than anything else, this has been the cause of the recent recession. Industry has taken advantage of the present situation and has increased prices to such an extent as to reduce the purchasing power of the people. The result has been another recession and increased unemployment. It will be noticed that when it rains in the United States, it is generally cloudy in Canada. Canada has not been affected to the same extent. According to the last returns I saw, the decrease in trade in the United States amounted to 26 per cent, whereas the decrease in Canada amounted to only around 6 per cent.
How can we increase employment? In view of the fact that in the last year industry has enjoyed prosperity, I believe men engaged in industry are in a reasonably sound financial position, and if they were given the right to distribute certain government funds we might get results by way of a solution of some relief problems, and might obtain more in this way than by handing out moneys in direct relief. I would suggest a survey of all industries, asking them to increase employment. So that hon. members may follow my observations, I shall use the unit of five per cent as indicating the desired increase in employment. We would pay the relief moneys to the experienced men who would be taken on. We would consider the agricultural implement business, for instance, as one of the basic industries. I mention that industry because the customers of it are the farmers, those people engaged in our primary industry. The government would subsidize purchases from the agricultural implement firm to the extent of twenty per cent. When the firm received an order from a farmer the purchase would be subsidized to that extent, on condition that the industry would reduce the price by a similar amount as the increased demand for goods would have a tendency to lower cost of production in industry. The scheme may look somewhat farfetched, but I believe it is workable.
Then, along another line, we know that many buildings in Canada are greatly in need

Relief and Agricultural Distress
of paint. If the same scheme were applied to paint companies, a great many men would be employed and at the same time we would be protecting national wealth. The same scheme could be applied to the textile industry, through the distribution of clothing. Furniture companies could benefit in the same way. I should be inclined to extend the scheme for a period of time to every young married couple, giving them the advantage of the subsidy in setting up their homes. The housing problem, the forestry problem, and all other problems which have been pointed out could work in conjunction with the scheme I have in mind. Then, I trust the minister will not overlook the extension of farm credits, because I believe a great deal more can be done along the line of extending credit to farmers, and especially to those farmers who have sons. The farm loan board would be well advised to give a little extra credit to the farmer who wishes to place his sons on farms. The family could be organized into a unit to work together. In my view it is much better to keep on the farm those boys who are already there, because the farmer who has come from the city has proved to be a failure. I hold the view that after the boy leaves the farm and goes to a city, there is not much chance for his ever becoming a successful farmer. For these reasons it would be wise to try to keep him on the farm.
As a consequence of the pump-priming scheme I have suggested, and after the return of greater prosperity, we would introduce a general welfare act. In the operation of the act there would be an assessment on every man's pay, which would be held out as payment for his own social security when he reaches an age when he cannot work. That, in itself, would relieve the burden of taxation upon land and buildings which to-day is militating against the building trades. Because of the extreme taxes people are reluctant to erect new buildings. The time has come when, no matter what station in life a man may hold, it is his duty to contribute, according to his ability, to his own general welfare, and I would suggest that when the minister brings down his unemployment insurance scheme he keep that fact in mind. I would suggest that such a measure include every man, whether he be on the farm or whether he be a labourer. A general welfare act would include farmers as well as labourers. From experience I have learned that a system of insurance equivalent to an old age pension would give security to those people who have reached the end of their working period, and would place them in a

position whereby they could live along the standards to which they are entitled. Today they may have their living, but that is about all.
On the statute books of Canada to-day there is a Government Annuities Act. Any young person who will contribute $20.62 yearly, from the age of twenty-one years, may, at the age of sixty-five years, have the equivalent of an old age pension. In the event of his death before the required age, all the money he has paid in, plus four per cent, will be returned. It would be impossible to have an unemployment insurance scheme which would give the proper treatment to the farmer; but by incorporating the Government Annuities Act in the social security plan I have outlined, the benefits would be extended to each and every citizen. I feel the time has come when, no matter what one's circumstances in life may be, it is necessary for the government to legislate for each and every one so that we may all go abreast, share in one another's joys and in one another's sorrows.
I remember that while I was a boy the insurance scheme was brought into existence in England, and I am sure there was great hostility shown towards it. I believe that was probably the beginning of my interest in public affairs. I read with a great deal of interest the observations made by Mr. David Lloyd George in connection with the insurance bill. He was then Chancellor of the Exchequer under the able leadership of Mr. Campbell-Bannerman. It was at that time he introduced the insurance measure, and the famous Lloyd George budget, at a time when industry in England would scarcely tolerate the suggestion of an insurance scheme. I believe hon. members will agree that nothing has contributed more to hold the people of Great Britain together than has the scheme of unemployment insurance brought down at that time despite the greatest opposition and hostility. I am not suggesting the figures I have indicated to-night are actuarially correct ; but it is my belief that if we are to have security, it is the duty of every man to make some contribution towards it. I believe that is sound social credit. The only difference is that you supply the medium from which you get the benefit, instead of getting the benefit and then, like Micawber, hoping something will turn up.

If people would be a little more self-reliant they could assist themselves and assist the government. I am not so sure that it is the function of government to do some of the things we are doing. subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS

There is already a great demand for goods and services in this country. People need many things which industry can supply, and we have the men who can produce and supply them and the materials with which to make these goods. It is all a matter of confidence; but confidence has been destroyed more or less by reason of the fact that for the last few years in civilized countries people have been getting on soap boxes and trying to expound some kind of ism, instead of getting into the boat of life, taking hold of the oars and pulling their own weight in the boat. They would rather be a big shot in some ism than contribute something to help the old ship of state along.
I hope I have not taken too long, and I do not know that in my contribution to this debate I have made myself clear; but I should like to throw out the suggestion that if we are going to get back to prosperity, every man must do something to contribute to his own social security. True, there are difficulties to surmount; but I believe that if we can relieve the burden of taxation on industry and lands and buildings, industry will forge ahead. Certainly industry cannot continue to bear
the burden it is bearing to-day. Industry is supporting itself and helping to support a large proportion of these people who ought to be contributing something towards the national wealth of this country.
While I believe with the Minister of Finance that Canadian people enjoy one of the highest standards of living in the civilized world, one of the difficulties under which we are labouring to-day is economic indigestion. Science and invention have flooded our civilization with so many of the luxuries of life that as a people we are often unable to resist accepting luxuries instead of being content with essentials, and a good deal of the product of our labour is ill spent. We are not putting it directly into the channels in which it will provide the necessities of life. We are spending a good deal of the product of our labours in luxuries instead of spending it upon the necessities of life, and that is responsible to a great extent for many of our present difficulties.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Would the hon. member say there is a scarcity of necessities?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS

No; there is no scarcity of necessities, but there is a scarcity of intelligence in people who purchase luxuries instead of necessities.
In closing my remarks, I would say that I believe the people are expecting an honest attempt to approach these questions, and I congratulate the government upon appointing the commissions which have been condemned by our hon. friends opposite. But it is just as necessary in the field of science, I am led to believe, to ascertain that a thing cannot be done as that a thing can be done, and I believe that as a result of their labours we shall ascertain what it is possible to do and that we shall forge ahead, having found a place to put our feet on the ground, rather than blundering into some abyss. There is a tendency, as I have felt while listening to hon. members opposite, to want action for action's sake. The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Poole) in his contribution a couple of weeks ago said: "For heaven's sake do something." I cannot agree with that attitude. I think it is much better to know just where you are going than to take a leap in the dark just to do something, and those who are responsible to the Canadian people for the government of this country must be very cautious and not just do something that might bring about disaster.

He asked us to go back into history. Perhaps he would like to have Julius Caesar as Prime Minister and Mark Antony as Minister of Finance. But civilization has progressed since the days of ancient Rome until the Liberal party came into power, and now things seem to be at a standstill.
The hon. member who spoke last (Mr. Wood) told us that unemployment could be solved; that it was up to the people who are unemployed. I wonder whether it is an epidemic of laziness that has afflicted this country. What was it that struck this dominion in 1929? Did many Canadians then decide to go on strike forever? The Minister of Labour has already told us that the solution of our problem is the expanding of trade, although the evidence in every part -of the world shows the trend is towards contracting markets. I was also struck to-night
fMr. Green.]
by members of the Liberal party turning to members of the opposition and asking for suggestions. When the Liberal party were elected, surely they had some idea as to how they were going to solve this problem, or did they, as an hon. member who has just spoken seems to think, just come here to sit? That is all that has happened in the last three sessions. They still have the problem before them. I do not know why the Minister of Labour hides the government's policy. I do not know what there is to hide. As a representative of the Canadian people I should like to know what the policy of the government is to be during the coming year.
