speechtext: I think it is the best country in the world, but I am here to make it a better country.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Another Mussolini.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Well, we are starting in the west, and it must be admitted that we have made a good start. We have taken one province, and next year we shall do more. I believe that the social credit forces in this country represent the hope of economic democracy in Canada.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
In the hon.
member's opinion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
And the promise of
twenty-five dollars a month to the electors.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
What were the Liberal
members elected on?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Your group did not intend to keep their promise.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Oh, no.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
The Liberal party promised
to issue credit for the public need and they did not do so. Let them be fair. Alberta is merely one province in the dominion, and if the social credit party of that province had the necessary power there is no question about what it would do. But the Liberal party has the power. My hon. friends opposite said that they would do certain things and they have not done them. For many years in this parliament there is one body of citizens who have not been represented and that is the poor people of Canada. I have always felt that the members did not understand the conditions under which the people were living. We have a tremendous debt which is being added to every year, every decade. In the last twenty years we have spent from all sources pretty close to a billion dollars for all kinds of relief. What could we not have done with that money in building useful public works and homes for the people? Have the government any vision of a future when unemployment will be a thing of the past, when once again there will be a demand for the youth of Canada in industry? If the government have not that vision, have they made provision for the youth of the country?
[Mr. Fournier. J
The Minister of Finance emphasized the fact that we promised $25 a month. I do not think there is any harm in promising $25 a month to every citizen. I believe the country is rich enough to provide every man, woman and1 child with food, clothing and shelter, but the Liberal party does not share that belief. I do not know why any child born into this world should not be assured a living the same as the birds of the air. I do not know why anybody should not benefit by the technological improvements that have been made by science, and certainly the great mass of the people who have helped through the generations to bring about fhat improvement are entitled to share in the oenefits. I do not know that the Almighty gave the monopolists of Canada an exclusive right to all the benefits accumulated through the generations. I have heard many eloquent pleas in this house for people who are always well defended because they have plenty of money. We are told not to touch sacred/ rights of bondholders, but when it comes to the unemployed it is a different matter entirely. If they send a delegation to some place in Toronto or to the capital city of Ottawa, they are only thrown into gaol.
I want to make this plain to the hon. gentleman who accuses me of being a fascist. If there were ever any party in this country that has done more than another towards creating unrest and discontent, it is the Liberal party. They have done this by the simple method of doing nothing in parliament; they have simply drifted down stream. Quite often when I speak in the house I have the same feeling that was expressed by an hon. gentleman this afternoon-it all seems so futile. It seems that we are dealing not with human beings, but with units, something abstract that does not concern parliament. But there are none so blind as those who will not see. A government that refuses to give the people of the country a living, a government that sits by and waits for something to happen in some other country, for another world war to absorb the unemployed, is not a government that can be commended. Such a policy does not speak highly for it. The government of this generation should be a planning government; it should know exactly where it is going; it should be planning from one five year period to another, and as the nation becomes wealthier every individual in the country should share in the benefits of that wealth.
There has been much criticism of social credit in this house, but I can assure you, Mr. Chairman, that it cannot be criticized out of existence. I should hate, however, to belong

Relief and Agricultural Distress
to a social credit party that advocated the sort of social credit that hon. members opposite understand and interpret. Social credit does not mean redistribution of existing purchasing power; it does not mean taking from one and giving to another. Social credit in its simplest form means this: that you cannot, under the present system, provide sufficient purchasing power at any one time to purchase total production as represented by prices. There is a difference between what it costs to produce and what the consumer is asked to pay for the product. Social credit represents the difference between what it costs to produce goods and the ultimate price of them. That is social credit in its simplest form.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: My hon. friend has been telling us what social credit is not; what we are waiting for is a definition of what it is.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
I have just told the hon. member. It is the difference between total cost of production and the ultimate price of the goods produced. I know that one of the ministers, speaking in the west recently, referred to the weird ideas of social credit. Well, you do not have to go beyond the Liberal party to find weird ideas; in fact, some of their ideas are real nightmares. They talk in this house about solving the unemployment problem, while the national credit they leave in the control of someone else. The Minister of Finance tells us that we control it, but we are not getting much of it. The people are not enjoying it even if we do control it. Nor is social credit scrip. Scrip is recoverable by taxation, and that is a different thing entirely. While on the subject of unemployment, I wonder if as Canadians-never mind where I came from-
Mr. ST-PERE:	According to the parliamentary guide the hon. gentleman came here when he was three years old, and he said he chose this country to live in. He was pretty precocious.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
I was in this country and in this city twenty-nine years ago.
Mr. ST-PERE: But the hon. member did
not choose this country to come to.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
No; in fact I went back.
Mr. ST-PERE:	He should apologize to
the hon. member.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
At the age of two years I left Canada, but I came back in 1928, so I did choose the country. I am sorry my hon. friend did not have the same privilege. But
this subject of unemployment is not something you can laugh out of existence. We need some money to deal with it. We need some public works. It makes no difference what hon. members opposite or on this side suggest, you cannot do anything without the instrument with which to do it, and in this case the economic instrument is national credit. I hope that in future in this house the Liberal party will not go as far back as ancient Rome to find a precedent for unemployment. Unless this government change their tactics and really do something, they will probably be the last democratic government in this country; democracy will pass from Canada as it passed from Europe, because governments refused to do the things which they knew were essential for the national welfare. People will not be found desiring change or dictatorships when they are contented. This government is responsible for making Canadians a contented people. The only way to make them contented is to absorb our youth into industry, once again imbue them with the spirit of Canadianism, make them feel that they are a part of society, doing their part in the building of a great nation.
Mr. ST-PERE: Hear, hear.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
I do not know what my hon. friend finds funny about that.
Mr. ST-PERE:	I said "Hear, hear." I
congratulate the hon. member.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
I wish my hon. friend would come out to my riding some time-
' Mr. ST-PERE:	I invite the hon. member
to mine.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
If they would visit the soup kitchens of Canada, hon. members would not find this such a light subject. If they would forego their sessional indemnity and bankbooks for a few weeks and go to the soup kitchens of Canada, they would understand these problems better. There is a job to do, and the people of Canada sent this government here to do it, not to wish away the problem of unemployment, but to do away with it. The way to do away with unemployment is to put people back to work, absorb them into building and construction. Unless a start is made, the outlook is poor for the people to enjoy the security which they have known even in these days of scarcity. So the slogan of this party now, while in office, should be: Work and wages; not relief and dole. Unemployment insurance does not appeal to me; it is only a palliative, something to string along with for another decade and get by without doing the real job that

Relief and Agricultural Distress
should be done. In Great Britain they have had unemployment insurance, but has it solved the problem there?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Do I understand that the hon. member is against a scheme of unemployment insurance in this country?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: I am very much opposed to unemployment insurance as suggested by this government.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Is the hon. gentleman opposed to a scheme of unemployment insurance as he understands this government is considering it?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Or any scheme of unemployment insurance that is known to us?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Yes; it is so unnecessary. It is nothing new; they have had it in Germany, in Great Britain. It is only a palliative.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Is the hon. gentleman speaking for himself, or his group?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: I am speaking for myself; the group is able to speak for itself.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: The group agree; they were prompting him.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: The government propose that, whether it is reasonable or not, as long as it is a vote-catcher. It would be only a redistribution of purchasing power, not a solution of the problem; only taking something from the person who is working so that the person who is not working may get some of it, making a man who may be getting $10 a week contribute part of that for the unemployed. The problem is the lack of purchasing power; if you redistribute the whole income of Canadians in terms of cash, it would not solve the problem. It is not a problem of redistribution.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: My hon. friend is opposed to the payment of $25 a month to people without any return given to the state?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
But the return has been given by generations past. Let me explain, if my hon. friend would like an explanation. The greatest, the most important factor in the economic system is the consumer. Unless he is getting and using goods, industry slows dowrn. You must place in the hands of the consumer effective demand. There is of course a difference between demand and effective demand; a million people in Canada to-day demand things but they do not get them because they have not the tokens or the effective demand in their hands. If the

consumer is recognized as the greatest factor, you must realize that they are short of purchasing power. To redistribute that which is already in the hands of people would not make up the deficiency in purchasing power; you must have more; you must begin with the consumer so that he begins to buy and drag goods from industry.
To-day we have arrived at the point where governments are stimulating industry. In the United States they are "priming the pump," giving loans to industry. But the managers of banks in Canada tell you that their problem is to make loans. Why? Because industry to-day has developed to a high degree its power of production so that it can produce more than the purchasing power which goes out in wages, salaries and dividends can absorb. So the social credit proposal is very simple: Begin with the consumer. It is because of the consumer that there is any economic activity at all. If a machine is put into a factory, this is done for only one purpose, to produce goods. The only reason for producing goods is that people may use them. To-day goods can be produced in great abundance; the reason we have a depression to-day is not because we cannot produce enough, but because the consumer has not the wherewithal, the effective demand, to take the goods from industry. It is of no use to pay it in wages, because that would increase prices. So you have to do two things: First, to give out purchasing power which does not pass into the cost accounting system, in other words, does not go into the cost of production, but begins with the consumer. The second thing is to stop the rise in prices. To do that you apply what is called a discount rate; you compensate the retailer or producer if he sells below the cost of production.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: How do you do that?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
By paying the difference
directly to the producer.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: What with? Where do you get it?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: National credit.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Do not laugh.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: It is impossible not to laugh.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
If hon. members want to know about social credit, we will tell them. The hon. member for Melfort asks where the money comes from. Let me ask him where any money comes from.

Relief and Agricultural Distress

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Money, as my hon. friend knows, is promissory notes. He knows that if he issues promissory notes beyond his capacity to pay, he will not get further credit. And the state would be in the same position.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Money is not a promissory note. No matter what money is made of, provided it has arrived at that degree of acceptability that you can exchange goods and services for it, it is money. It is valueless unless it has a demand quality, unless you can exchange it for goods. A fe,w moments ago my hon. friend asked me what was behind it and where it came from. The credit which would be used in social credit would be exactly the same as you use to-day, and the very same things would be behind it-goods and services. We have said already that there is an insufficient purchasing power and that we want to increase that purchasing power. The goods and services behind that increase would be just the same as what is behind yoiur money to-day.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: My hon. friend admits that there would be a natural rise in prices as a result of the initial application of this principle and he acknowledges that unless there was effective price control, things would get out of hand. The just price or price control is an essential feature of his theory. I gather it is the intention to bring about that control ,by paying to the seller the difference between what he would have to charge as a result of the higher prices and what would be regarded by some authority as a just price. Am I correct in that? There would be paid to the retailer the difference between what the goods cost him as a result of the price enhancement, on .the one hand, and what was determined by some authority to be the just price, on the other.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: I would say that is correct.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
Then I am correct so
far. My hon. friend then says that the money to be paid to the retailer under these circumstances is to be national credit; that is, it is to be based upon, the production of goods and services. However, already we have produced those goods at too high a price; we have already used the national credit in producing them and in creating the just price which we are going to bonu3 the retailer for charging. What would be the basis for the credit which would be issued by the state for that secondary purpose? Two and two still make four.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
There is a logical answer to these questions.
Mr. MaoINNIS: I would suggest that the Minister of Finance carry his question just a point further. He should point out that the additional credit which would be paid to the retailer would further increase inflation.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
The Minister of Finance
suggested that in the initial stage prices would rise. That is natural. To-day some goods are sold for which fair prices are not received. We would have to arrive at a price level which would give the seller or the producer his cost plus something else, commission or profit. I think the idea that the world can never operate without a profit is absurd, because to me anything over and above cost is profit. I think the minister is overlooking one thing. He said that when you have produced goods you have used up your national credit. That is not true.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: To that extent.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: To the extent of the cost, but not to the extent of the price.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: My hon. friend made a point of the fact that the cost would be too high.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: The price.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: He proposed a bonus to bring down the price resulting from the too high costs.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: Let me put it to the minister in this way. An article might be selling to-day for a dollar which might be considered a fair price which a retailer receives under the present competitive system. With a social credit scheme in operation, that article would sell for seventy-five cents. We would be increasing the value of money on the one hand, and we would be giving the consumer more money, on the other. That is true, is it not? If I sell an article for seventy-five cents which sold previously for a dollar and the state compensates me as the retailer, I would lose nothing. However, the consumer would be able to purchase more goods with his money. That does away with your theory of inflation. You could not possibly have inflation if prices come down to the consumer as you produce more.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
I should like to ask a question in connection with what the hon. gentleman has just said. There would still be countries in the world in which social credit would not be in operation. Having in mind our economic interdependence, how are you going to deal with the inevitable variation in price? How are you going to deal with the price level?

Relief and Agricultural Distress

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
As we deal with it to-day.
Theoretically in international trade we deal in terms of cash, but actually we deal in terms of goods. All we do in foreign trade is to exchange goods for goods. I know that we have sold goods to China, but I have never seen Chinese money in this country. It is true that there will be a difference between the price of goods here and the price of goods in other countries, but there is a difference to-day. Adjustments will be made in exactly the same way. We do not intend to interfere with anything internationally; this is a scheme which works internally.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
Assuming that this social
credit state was a debtor country, how would you meet your obligations to creditor nations?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: We are a debtor nation today and we meet our debts in the old-fashioned way, by exporting more goods. We pay in terms of goods and services. We have possibly one of the finest examples of that in the manner in which Germany attempted to pay her debts to the United States. She paid with boots and shoes and the United States worker who came back from France found that he was out of a job. We do that now and we shall do it to-morrow. Under social credit our national debt would be reduced because we would have more goods for export. We would be producing more because the demand would be greater. The demand for imports would be greater because we do not produce that variety which is necessary to national need.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
How would you pay for
your imports?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
The same as we do to-day,
with our exports. There is no other way in which you could pay for them.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
Supposing citizen "A"
wanted to buy shoes from Czechoslovakia, how would the transaction be carried on under social credit?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
In exactly the same way
as it would to-day. His cheque would go into the clearing house and be charged against this country.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
Supposing the shoes cost
one hundred dollars. How much would the citizen in the social credit country have to pay to the exporting country?

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: I do not understand.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: The state is going to increase the purchasing power of the citizen; the state is going to pay a portion of the cost of that commodity.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: I did not say that.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
That is what the hon.
member has said.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
No. We were discussing
placing money in the hands of the purchaser. You pay it into the hands of the consumer.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
The man who buys the
shoes is the consumer.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext: The man in this country.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
In international trade we
would pay for things just as we do now. Does the hon. member suggest there is no difference between the prices of goods produced in Canada and the prices in some other countries? They are not the same in any other nation of the world.
But that does not enter into the argument with respect to social credit, and I shall discard it. We are talking about national credit which will make up the difference in the cost of production and ultimate prices and which will supply the consumer with things which could not possibly be purchased through the cost and price system as we know it to-day.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
At this point could we
not get back to the section under discussion? Everybody has had an innings. I admire the courage of the hon. member who has just spoken. He has gone further than most of his colleagues in the development of the social credit theory, but after all that discussion does not really fall within the four corners of the section before the committee.

subtopic: MEASURE FOR ALLEVIATION OF UNEMPLOYMENT AND AGRICULTURAL DISTRESS
speechtext:
I would remind the minister that we claim the problem cannot be solved without social credit. Hon. members opposite have asked certain questions which I have been only too pleased to answer.
In conclusion, I say that until we recognize that there is a deficiency of purchasing power, and that all our industrial activity is for one purpose and one only, namely to supply the ultimate consumer with the goods of production, we shall not reach a satisfactory solution. That is the purpose of the economic system. If it is not, then I want hon. members opposite to tell me why we produce goods.
Debate on the question of money cannot be had too often. It is the first and most important question which can ever come before parliament in this day and generation. Until a political party which will deal with money and credit sits on the right side of Mr. Speaker, we shall never get out of the present economic chaos. As one of the youngest men in the house may I say that I fear the future, under present governmental policy. I can see no hope and I can see contracting markets -the very thing which will destroy all the

Privilege-Mr. Church
doctrines of the old line parties. We find Japan making inroads into China, with the result that industrialization takes place and less is bought from us. Germany goes into Austria, industrializes it and buys less from us. Italy goes into Abyssinia, industrializes it and buys less from us. We are faced with a greater paradox than ever. Here is a nation choked with wealth and the machinery to produce vast quantities of the very things which people want, but they cannot buy.
That is all I have to say on the matter. I thank hon. members for the questions they have asked. I am so convinced that the monetary system is wrong that I avail myself of every opportunity I get to go to any county or school district to tell the people something about this monetary system which keeps humanity shackled to poverty.

Progress reported.
